Five behaviors of binding and catalysis, derived and placed

The full five-step comparison for each behavior, then every result placed at its parameter conditions, read backwards for design, and bounded by what the regime enumeration of a written mechanism guarantees.

CCBS · Lecture 9 · exposition · 7 October 2026

This chapter is the derivation companion to the core. The core shows five behaviors that cells build from binding and catalysis: the sign of regulation, a threshold, memory, adaptation and a rhythm. It explains each one by the allocation of a finite pool. Here each behavior is derived in full, with every model written out, every limit taken explicitly and every number traced to a calculation. Nothing below assumes an equation from the core.

The chapter has one method and one destination. The method is a five-step comparison between a binding-catalysis model and the effective rate law usually written in its place. The destination is a table that puts each example, and each published result about the same behavior, at the parameter conditions where it holds. A reader who finishes should be able to take a mechanism this page never mentions, run the five steps, and place a result on that table.

Parts 2 to 6 run the comparison on the five behaviors, one part each. Part 7 collects them. It shows that every boundary on the placement table has been derived, reads the table backwards for design, and states what the enumeration of regimes guarantees about a written mechanism and what it leaves to the closed dynamics. The lineage tells how the field reached each verdict. This page cites the literature for authority only.

Conventions

A bare species symbol is a free concentration: XX, RR, PP. A total, the sum over every state that contains a constituent, is qXq_X. A complex of A and B is CABC_{AB}, and the dissociation constant of a pair is KdK_d, or a labelled K when a page carries several. An elementary step gets a straight arrow with its microscopic constants. A composite step, such as transcription, translation, degradation or dilution, gets a bare squiggle, and its rate law is written beside it.

Every number carries one of four labels, stated where it appears. Exact means exact within the stated reduced model, usually a closed form. Leading order means a limit or a dominance approximation, with its condition named. Numerical means a model prediction computed at stated illustrative parameters. Reported means a measurement or a stated value in a cited source, with its page. No number here is a fit to data.

Part 1

A fair comparison

What is compared, how an effective law sits inside a binding-catalysis model, and what matching the two can and cannot fix.

1A behavior is a property of the closed loop

A response curve describes one experiment on a binding layer. A behavior belongs to the vector field on the totals, once production and removal close the loop.

The object of comparison is a vector field on totals, so we build one concretely first. Take a protein X that binds one partner Y. Binding is the elementary pair

X+Y⇌k−k+CXY,Kd=k−k+,X+Y\xrightleftharpoons[k_-]{k_+}C_{XY},\qquad K_d=\frac{k_-}{k_+},(1)

where k+k_+ is the association rate constant, k−k_- the dissociation rate constant, and KdK_d their ratio, the dissociation constant, a concentration. Binding moves molecules between states without changing how many X there are. The totals count every state:

qX=X+CXY,qY=Y+CXY.q_X=X+C_{XY},\qquad q_Y=Y+C_{XY}.(2)

Binding is fast against everything else, so at every instant the pair sits at equilibrium, KdCXY=XYK_dC_{XY}=XY. Given the totals, eqs. (1) and (2) fix every free species and complex. That is Lecture 8's binding layer.

Production and removal change the totals, and that closes the loop. Suppose X is made by a composite step whose rate law vprodv_\mathrm{prod} depends on the binding layer, for instance on how much of a promoter is free. Its total then obeys an addition-removal balance:

q˙X=vprod(q;b)−(removal of every X-containing state).\dot q_X=v_\mathrm{prod}(q;b)-(\text{removal of every X-containing state}).(3)

Here q collects the totals and b the binding constants and activities. The binding layer computes the production law from the totals, and the balance moves the totals. A behavior is what this closed loop does.

The removal term has a rule, and the rule is part of the model. If free X is removed at frequency λf\lambda_\mathrm{f} and bound X at λb\lambda_\mathrm{b}, the loss is λfX+λbCXY\lambda_\mathrm{f}X+\lambda_\mathrm{b}C_{XY}. We write θ=λb/λf\theta=\lambda_\mathrm{b}/\lambda_\mathrm{f} for the bound-to-free removal ratio. Growth dilution removes every state alike, so θ=1\theta=1 and the loss is λqX\lambda q_X, a function of the total alone. Removal of free X only, for example by a protease that cannot reach bound X, has θ=0\theta=0, and binding then protects X. These are the two variants Lecture 8's coda handed over. Part 6 shows that the whole range of θ\theta matters.

A behavior is one of four properties of that vector field. It can be how a steady state depends on a total, how many attractors exist, how far the output returns after a sustained step of input, or whether a stable cycle exists. The first is a static input-output behavior and the other three are dynamical. A steep response curve of the binding layer alone, measured at fixed totals, is a static relation of that layer, and a count of binding states is a property of the layer too. The loop can turn either into different closed-loop behaviors or into none.

Each comparison in this chapter runs five steps, and each step removes one ambiguity.

  1. Model. Write the elementary binding steps, the composite production and removal steps with their rate laws, the totals, the removal rule and the observable.
  2. Limit. Derive the effective rate law as a limit of that model, and name the assumptions that make it exact.
  3. Match. Choose parameters so that both give the same response at one reference condition.
  4. Move a total. Change what a cell changes: an input total, a regulator total, a site number, a removal rate.
  5. Close the loop. Read the behavior from the closed dynamics: steady states, their stability, the error after a step, or a cycle.

Two of the five steps exist to keep the comparison fair, and two to make it informative. Step 2 makes the effective law a correct answer to a narrower question, not a strawman. Step 3 prevents a difference of scale from posing as a difference of mechanism. Step 4 is where the two models can part. Step 5 decides whether the parting is a difference in behavior.

State a behavior as a property of the closed vector field on the totals, with the removal rule named by its bound-to-free ratio θ\theta, and plan every comparison as model, limit, match, move a total, close the loop.

2One binding pair supplies the elementary calculation

Most effective laws in this chapter are the binding pair of eq. (1) evaluated in one of its regimes, and the multisite and multimer laws of Parts 3 and 4 are assembled from the same calculation. Drawn on the pair's map, a law is a cut that stays on one side of a boundary.

The pair has an exact solution, and the effective laws are its limits. Write the pair generically as E+S⇌k−k+CESE+S\xrightleftharpoons[k_-]{k_+}C_{ES}, with totals qE=E+CESq_E=E+C_{ES} and qS=S+CESq_S=S+C_{ES}. Substituting E=qE−CESE=q_E-C_{ES} and S=qS−CESS=q_S-C_{ES} into KdCES=ESK_dC_{ES}=ES gives a quadratic, CES2−TCES+qEqS=0C_{ES}^2-TC_{ES}+q_Eq_S=0 with T=qE+qS+KdT=q_E+q_S+K_d. Its physical root is the smaller one, written without a cancelling difference:

CES=2qEqST+T2−4qEqS.C_{ES}=\frac{2q_Eq_S}{T+\sqrt{T^2-4q_Eq_S}}.(4)

The root lies between zero and the smaller total, as a complex must.

Lecture 8 sorts the pair into four regimes by which term wins each total. A regime names the winner of qEq_E first, then the winner of qSq_S. Keeping only the winners and the binding relation gives one monomial law per regime. Each law is accurate to leading order deep inside its sector, where the stated inequalities hold with a wide margin:

RegimeLeading-order lawSector where the law is accurate
(E,S)(E,S)CES≈qEqS/KdC_{ES}\approx q_Eq_S/K_dqE≪Kdq_E\ll K_d and qS≪Kdq_S\ll K_d
(E,CES)(E,C_{ES})CES≈qSC_{ES}\approx q_S, S≈KdqS/qES\approx K_dq_S/q_EqS≪qEq_S\ll q_E and qE≫Kdq_E\gg K_d
(CES,S)(C_{ES},S)CES≈qEC_{ES}\approx q_E, E≈KdqE/qSE\approx K_dq_E/q_SqE≪qSq_E\ll q_S and qS≫Kdq_S\gg K_d
(CES,CES)(C_{ES},C_{ES})E≈S≈KdqEE\approx S\approx\sqrt{K_dq_E}qE≫Kdq_E\gg K_d and ∣qE−qS∣≪KdqE|q_E-q_S|\ll\sqrt{K_dq_E}

The last regime is singular, and for a structural reason. The complex wins both totals, so the two winner equations, CES≈qEC_{ES}\approx q_E and CES≈qSC_{ES}\approx q_S, select the same column and leave E and S undetermined. Its law needs one more balance. The difference of the totals is exact, qE−qS=E−Sq_E-q_S=E-S, so near the ray E≈SE\approx S, and binding gives ES=KdCES≈KdqEES=K_dC_{ES}\approx K_dq_E. A small free pool of size KdqE\sqrt{K_dq_E} survives where nearly everything is bound. The condition E≈SE\approx S needs the difference of the totals to be small on that scale, not merely the totals to look close on a log plot.

The sector lines are leading-order boundaries, not exact ties. An exact tie is an equal contribution of two terms to one total. Free and bound E contribute equally where CES=qE/2C_{ES}=q_E/2, and binding then forces S=KdS=K_d, so the tie lies on the curve qS=Kd+qE/2q_S=K_d+q_E/2. Free and bound S tie on qE=Kd+qS/2q_E=K_d+q_S/2. The leading-order map draws the first of these as qS=max⁡(Kd,qE)q_S=\max(K_d,q_E), which differs from the exact curve by at most a factor of 2. Lecture 8 guaranteed agreement within such bounded factors and no more. A tie marks a boundary between two regimes. It is a different thing from the singular regime above, where the winners are dependent.

The Michaelis-Menten law is the pair wherever the free substrate wins its own total. If S≈qSS\approx q_S, then E=qE−CESE=q_E-C_{ES} and KdCES=(qE−CES)qSK_dC_{ES}=(q_E-C_{ES})q_S give

CES≈qE qSKd+qS.C_{ES}\approx q_E\,\frac{q_S}{K_d+q_S}.(5)

The condition S≈qSS\approx q_S holds in the regimes (E,S)(E,S) and (CES,S)(C_{ES},S), that is when qS≫qEq_S\gg q_E or Kd≫qEK_d\gg q_E. This validity condition is the one Liu, Ren and Xiao derived for the law.1 Outside it the substrate is held in the complex, and eq. (5) has no way to say so.

The Hill law with coefficient 1 is the free partner on a weak cut. Hold qEq_E far below KdK_d, the partner in trace, and sweep qSq_S. The free species S then wins its total, so CES/E=S/Kd≈qS/KdC_{ES}/E=S/K_d\approx q_S/K_d, and the free fraction of the partner is

EqE≈KdKd+qS.\frac{E}{q_E}\approx\frac{K_d}{K_d+q_S}.(6)

This is a repression law of Hill coefficient 1 in the total qSq_S. Its log-slope, −dln⁡(E/qE)/dln⁡qS=qS/(Kd+qS)-d\ln(E/q_E)/d\ln q_S=q_S/(K_d+q_S), never reaches 1. A promoter in trace read by a repressor is this cut.

A titration switch is the same partner on a tight cut. Hold qEq_E far above KdK_d. Below the ray, where qE−qS≫KdqEq_E-q_S\gg\sqrt{K_dq_E}, the complex holds nearly all of S, and the free partner falls only as the sites fill, E≈qE−qSE\approx q_E-q_S. Above it, where qS−qE≫KdqEq_S-q_E\gg\sqrt{K_dq_E}, the complex holds nearly all of E, the free S is qS−qEq_S-q_E, and E≈KdqE/(qS−qE)E\approx K_dq_E/(q_S-q_E). The (CES,S)(C_{ES},S) law E≈KdqE/qSE\approx K_dq_E/q_S needs the further excess qS≫qEq_S\gg q_E. Between these the free partner drops by a factor of order qE/Kdq_E/K_d, passing through KdqE\sqrt{K_dq_E} on the ray. A promoter pool read by a repressor whose total passes the pool is this cut, and Parts 4 and 6 use it.

Only the winners of the conservation sums are a dominance regime. A regime is a choice of one winning term per total, nothing more. The observable, the controlled input and the removal rule are separate model choices. A different observable reads the same allocation differently, as free and total output do in Part 5. A different removal rule changes the vector field without changing any allocation. A different architecture changes the conservation sums themselves. All four must be named to interpret a result, and only the first is a regime.

A cut's height decides the kind of response, and the height is a ratio of totals to KdK_d. Below the corner a cut breaks once, at qS=Kdq_S=K_d, where one total changes winner, and the response is graded. Above it a cut crosses the singular ray, where in the leading-order map both totals change winner together, and the response switches. At finite binding the two exact ties stay distinct: on a cut at fixed qE≫Kdq_E\gg K_d they sit near qS=qE/2q_S=q_E/2 and qS=2qEq_S=2q_E. Between them lies a broad intermediate band, and the free partner's collapse is concentrated in a much narrower rounding layer of width about KdqE\sqrt{K_dq_E} around the ray. Lecture 11 develops the general geometry of such maps for networks with many pairs. This chapter needs only the one-pair map, applied once per example.

Locate an effective law as a cut through a binding pair's map: name the regime it stays in, write the condition on the totals that keeps it there, and predict a switch wherever a path crosses the singular ray.

3Matching fixes one scale and leaves the totals free

Matching two models at a reference condition sets one constant for each quantity matched. It does not make the models equivalent, because it says nothing about how either one stores a total.

A match sets as many constants as it equates. To match a floor, a ceiling and a midpoint of two response curves, one chooses three parameters. The choice is a calibration, a fact about the parameters, not about the mechanisms. The binding-catalysis supplement of the lecturer's group makes the same point about a matched pair of induction circuits: the equality of the fitted curves is a calibration choice, not an identity of the full equilibrium.2

A match leaves three things free. It leaves the inventories: how much of each total sits in complexes rather than free. It leaves the joint states, such as which promoter states coexist. And it leaves the response to a total the match did not touch. Step 4 moves exactly such a total.

A match can move the two models to opposite sides of a regime boundary. Part 2 matches an induced activator to an induced repressor in free inducer. The match forces the activator to bind its inducer about 10410^4 times more weakly than the repressor does. On the map of Figure 1, it puts the activator's inducer pair near the corner and the repressor's far above it. The two circuits then answer a change of inducer total in opposite ways, and the match itself predicted it.

A contrast is stated with its conditions, and only a counterexample under those conditions refutes it. Each contrast below names its model, its observable, its controlled input, its removal rule and the one parameter it moves. A reproduced counterexample under exactly those statements would refute that contrast. A second successful fit of the effective law refutes nothing. The law should keep working wherever its regime holds, and it can agree by accident outside it.

After matching two models, list what the match fixed and which totals it left free, check where each model's pairs sit on the map, and state every contrast with the conditions a counterexample would have to meet.

Part 2

Sign of regulation

An inducer can turn a gene on through an activator or through a repressor. Matched in free inducer, the two circuits compute different functions of the inducer total. The core draws the two circuits side by side.

4The repressor circuit reduces to one equation

A repressor circuit has five binding species, but its equilibrium is one monotone equation for the free repressor, and its output reads that free repressor.

1 · Model, repressor. The job is to switch on a gene, the output protein G, when an inducer I appears. The repressor R binds the promoter D and blocks expression. The inducer binds the repressor, and the complex CRIC_{RI} cannot bind the promoter. The binding steps are elementary, and expression and removal are composite:

R+I⇌k−RIk+RICRI,D+R⇌k−DRk+DRCDR,D⇝D+G  (rate law aD),G⇝∅  (rate law δqG).\begin{aligned}&R+I\xrightleftharpoons[k_{-RI}]{k_{+RI}}C_{RI},\qquad D+R\xrightleftharpoons[k_{-DR}]{k_{+DR}}C_{DR},\\ &D\rightsquigarrow D+G\ \ (\text{rate law }aD),\qquad G\rightsquigarrow\varnothing\ \ (\text{rate law }\delta q_G).\end{aligned}(7)

Here a is the expression activity of a free promoter and δ\delta the removal frequency of the output. The two dissociation constants are KRI=k−RI/k+RIK_{RI}=k_{-RI}/k_{+RI} and KDR=k−DR/k+DRK_{DR}=k_{-DR}/k_{+DR}. The letter pair in a subscript names the partners. At equilibrium KRICRI=RIK_{RI}C_{RI}=RI and KDRCDR=DRK_{DR}C_{DR}=DR, and the three totals are

qR=R+CDR+CRI,qI=I+CRI,qD=D+CDR.q_R=R+C_{DR}+C_{RI},\qquad q_I=I+C_{RI},\qquad q_D=D+C_{DR}.(8)

Every species follows from the free repressor. The promoter total and its binding relation give D=qDKDR/(KDR+R)D=q_DK_{DR}/(K_{DR}+R) and CDR=qDR/(KDR+R)C_{DR}=q_DR/(K_{DR}+R). The inducer total gives, in the same way, CRI=qIR/(KRI+R)C_{RI}=q_IR/(K_{RI}+R). Substituting both into the repressor total leaves one equation for R:

R+qDRKDR+R+qIRKRI+R=qR.R+\frac{q_DR}{K_{DR}+R}+\frac{q_IR}{K_{RI}+R}=q_R.(9)

The left side rises strictly with R, from zero at R=0R=0 to at least qRq_R at R=qRR=q_R. So eq. (9) has exactly one root in (0,qR](0,q_R], for every set of totals.

The output reads the free repressor. Production is v=aDv=aD, so the production per promoter, in units of the free-promoter activity, is

va qD=KDRKDR+R.\frac{v}{a\,q_D}=\frac{K_{DR}}{K_{DR}+R}.(10)

This is the observable throughout Part 2. Because it reads a free species, it inherits the titration switch of §2 whenever the inducer total drives the free repressor across a ray.

The illustrative parameters put the repressor far above its operator constant. In nanomolar, qR=100q_R=100, KDR=1K_{DR}=1, KRI=0.01K_{RI}=0.01 and qD=0.1q_D=0.1, a trace promoter. The excess of the repressor over its operator constant is ρ=qR/KDR=100\rho=q_R/K_{DR}=100. These are model parameters chosen for clarity, not measurements.

Reduce a one-promoter repressor circuit to the single monotone equation (9) for the free repressor, and read its output as the free-promoter fraction (10).

5The activator circuit reduces to one equation, and its order is capped

The activator circuit also reduces to one equation, for the inducer-bound activator. Its output is a complex, and a complex holding one inducer can never rise faster than the inducer total.

1 · Model, activator. The activator A binds the inducer, and only the complex CAIC_{AI} binds the promoter, as CDAIC_{DAI}. The free activator cannot bind the promoter. Both promoter states express:

A+I⇌k−AIk+AICAI,D+CAI⇌k−DAk+DACDAI,D⇝D+G  (rate law a0D),CDAI⇝CDAI+G  (rate law a1CDAI),G⇝∅  (rate law δqG).\begin{aligned}&A+I\xrightleftharpoons[k_{-AI}]{k_{+AI}}C_{AI},\qquad D+C_{AI}\xrightleftharpoons[k_{-DA}]{k_{+DA}}C_{DAI},\\ &D\rightsquigarrow D+G\ \ (\text{rate law }a_0D),\quad C_{DAI}\rightsquigarrow C_{DAI}+G\ \ (\text{rate law }a_1C_{DAI}),\quad G\rightsquigarrow\varnothing\ \ (\text{rate law }\delta q_G).\end{aligned}(11)

The constants a0a_0 and a1a_1 are the activities of the free and the loaded promoter. At equilibrium KAICAI=AIK_{AI}C_{AI}=AI and KDACDAI=DCAIK_{DA}C_{DAI}=DC_{AI}, with totals

qA=A+CAI+CDAI,qI=I+CAI+CDAI,qD=D+CDAI.q_A=A+C_{AI}+C_{DAI},\qquad q_I=I+C_{AI}+C_{DAI},\qquad q_D=D+C_{DAI}.(12)

Every species follows from the inducer-bound activator. Write c=CAIc=C_{AI}. The promoter gives CDAI=qDc/(KDA+c)C_{DAI}=q_Dc/(K_{DA}+c). Let s(c)=c+CDAIs(c)=c+C_{DAI} be what the complexes hold of both the activator and the inducer. Then A=qA−s(c)A=q_A-s(c) and I=qI−s(c)I=q_I-s(c), and the binding relation of the pair becomes

(qA−s(c))(qI−s(c))=KAI c.\big(q_A-s(c)\big)\big(q_I-s(c)\big)=K_{AI}\,c .(13)

The left side falls and the right side rises as c grows from zero to the point where s(c)=min⁡(qA,qI)s(c)=\min(q_A,q_I). So eq. (13) has one root. The production is v=a0D+a1CDAI=a0qD+(a1−a0)CDAIv=a_0D+a_1C_{DAI}=a_0q_D+(a_1-a_0)C_{DAI}, and the rise above the floor is proportional to the active complex.

The active complex never rises faster than the inducer total, and the proof takes two observations. First, the share of the inducer that sits in the active complex depends only on the free activator and the free promoter. Second, both fall when inducer is added. Take the first. Every species is a product of free constituents, CAI=AI/KAIC_{AI}=AI/K_{AI} and CDAI=DAI/(KAIKDA)C_{DAI}=DAI/(K_{AI}K_{DA}), so the free inducer cancels from the share:

CDAIqI=DA/(KAIKDA)1+A/KAI+DA/(KAIKDA).\frac{C_{DAI}}{q_I}=\frac{DA/(K_{AI}K_{DA})}{1+A/K_{AI}+DA/(K_{AI}K_{DA})}.(14)

This share rises with A and with D.

The second observation follows from the Jacobian of the totals, which is positive definite. Differentiate the totals with respect to the logarithms of the free constituents A, I and D. Each species contributes its concentration once for every constituent it contains, so the Jacobian is the symmetric matrix

M=(qACAI+CDAICDAICAI+CDAIqICDAICDAICDAIqD),d (qA,qI,qD)T=M d (ln⁡A,ln⁡I,ln⁡D)T.M=\begin{pmatrix}q_A&C_{AI}+C_{DAI}&C_{DAI}\\ C_{AI}+C_{DAI}&q_I&C_{DAI}\\ C_{DAI}&C_{DAI}&q_D\end{pmatrix},\qquad d\,(q_A,q_I,q_D)^{\mathsf T}=M\,d\,(\ln A,\ln I,\ln D)^{\mathsf T}.(15)

It is positive definite, because for any vector w the form wTMww^{\mathsf T}Mw is a sum of species concentrations times squares. Adding inducer at fixed qAq_A and qDq_D changes the free logarithms by M−1M^{-1} times (0,dqI,0)(0,dq_I,0). The two entries of M−1M^{-1} that matter are cofactors:

(M−1)AI=−(CAI+CDAI) qD−CDAI 2det⁡M≤0,(M−1)DI=−CDAI Adet⁡M≤0.\big(M^{-1}\big)_{AI}=-\frac{(C_{AI}+C_{DAI})\,q_D-C_{DAI}^{\,2}}{\det M}\le0,\qquad \big(M^{-1}\big)_{DI}=-\frac{C_{DAI}\,A}{\det M}\le0.(16)

The first numerator is nonnegative because qD≥CDAIq_D\ge C_{DAI}. So free activator and free promoter both fall as the inducer total rises, the share (14) falls, and

0≤dln⁡CDAIdln⁡qI≤1.0\le\frac{d\ln C_{DAI}}{d\ln q_I}\le1 .(17)

The lower bound holds because CDAI=qD−DC_{DAI}=q_D-D rises as D falls. This is exact for every parameter set of the circuit (11), promoter loading included.

An order of at most 1 caps the Hill coefficient at 2. Measure steepness by nH=ln⁡81/ln⁡(EC90/EC10)n_H=\ln81/\ln(\mathrm{EC}_{90}/\mathrm{EC}_{10}), where EC10\mathrm{EC}_{10} and EC90\mathrm{EC}_{90} are the inputs giving 10% and 90% of the rise. The normalized rise is CDAI/CDAImax⁡C_{DAI}/C_{DAI}^{\max}, and by eq. (17) its log-slope is at most 1. A ninefold rise of the response, from 0.1 to 0.9, then needs at least a ninefold rise of input. So EC90/EC10≥9\mathrm{EC}_{90}/\mathrm{EC}_{10}\ge9 and nH≤ln⁡81/ln⁡9=2n_H\le\ln81/\ln9=2, whatever the parameters. The repressor's output (10) reads a free species, which carries no such bound. The lecturer's thesis states the general form of this dichotomy: an activating regulator acts through a complex, whose order in a total is bounded between 0 and 1, while a repressing regulator acts through a free species, whose order can become arbitrarily negative under tight binding.3

Reduce the activator circuit to eq. (13), and bound its response without computing it: the active complex has order at most 1 in the inducer total, so its Hill coefficient in that total is at most 2.

6Three assumptions give one free-inducer law

With binding at equilibrium, the free inducer clamped and the promoter in trace, both circuits become one Michaelis-Menten law with a floor. Matching them costs one affinity ratio of about 10410^4.

2 · Limit. Three assumptions give the usual effective law. Binding is at equilibrium. The free inducer I is the controlled input, as when a large medium holds it fixed. The transcription factor far exceeds the promoter, qD≪qRq_D\ll q_R and qD≪qAq_D\ll q_A, so loading the promoter does not deplete the factor. The fast subsystem removed is the binding layer, justified by binding equilibrium. The promoter in trace is a dominance choice: the factor wins its own total.

The repressor circuit becomes Michaelis-Menten in free inducer, with a floor. With the promoter in trace, the free repressor is the share of its total that holds no inducer, R=qRKRI/(KRI+I)R=q_RK_{RI}/(K_{RI}+I). Substituting into eq. (10) and rearranging,

va qD=11+ρ+ρ1+ρ IKeff+I,Keff=KRI(1+ρ).\frac{v}{a\,q_D}=\frac{1}{1+\rho}+\frac{\rho}{1+\rho}\,\frac{I}{K_\mathrm{eff}+I},\qquad K_\mathrm{eff}=K_{RI}(1+\rho).(18)

The floor 1/(1+ρ)1/(1+\rho) is the leak of a repressed promoter, and the rise above it is half complete at the free inducer KeffK_\mathrm{eff}.

The activator circuit becomes the same form. With the promoter in trace, the inducer-bound activator is c=qAI/(KAI+I)c=q_AI/(K_{AI}+I), and the loaded fraction of the promoter is c/(KDA+c)c/(K_{DA}+c). With ρA=qA/KDA\rho_A=q_A/K_{DA} that fraction rearranges to ρA1+ρA I/(KAI/(1+ρA)+I)\tfrac{\rho_A}{1+\rho_A}\,I/(K_{AI}/(1+\rho_A)+I). The production per promoter is (a0/a)(a_0/a) times the free fraction plus (a1/a)(a_1/a) times the loaded fraction. Its half-rise point is KAI/(1+ρA)K_{AI}/(1+\rho_A).

3 · Match. Three choices make the two laws identical. Give both factors the same excess, ρA=ρ=100\rho_A=\rho=100. Set the activities so that the floors and ceilings agree: the floor needs a0=a/(1+ρ)a_0=a/(1+\rho), and a ceiling of 1 then needs a1=a(2+ρ)/(1+ρ)a_1=a(2+\rho)/(1+\rho). Equal half-rise points need

KAI1+ρ=KRI(1+ρ)⟺KAI=(1+ρ)2KRI.\frac{K_{AI}}{1+\rho}=K_{RI}(1+\rho)\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad K_{AI}=(1+\rho)^2K_{RI}.(19)

At the illustrative parameters KAI=102.01 nMK_{AI}=102.01\ \mathrm{nM} and Keff=1.01 nMK_\mathrm{eff}=1.01\ \mathrm{nM} in both circuits. The exact circuits then agree with each other and with eq. (18) within 0.1% (numerical, Figure 2, left).

The match moves the two inducer pairs to opposite sides of the corner. Eq. (19) makes the repressor bind its inducer (1+ρ)2≈104(1+\rho)^2\approx10^4 times more tightly than the activator does. Excess activator lowers the half-rise point, because a few induced activators already fill the promoter. Excess repressor raises it, because nearly all of the repressor must be inactivated. On the map of Figure 1, the activator and its inducer sit at qA/KAI≈0.98q_A/K_{AI}\approx0.98, at the corner, and the repressor and its inducer at qR/KRI=104q_R/K_{RI}=10^4, far above it. The first cut is graded and the second switches, and §7 confirms both.

In this regime the two designs differ only in the sign of one sensitivity. Savageau compared activator and repressor control in systems that were otherwise identical, and found that the only inherent difference was their response to regulatory mutations (p. 5647).4 In eq. (18) and its activator twin, a change of the regulator's own total is such a mutation. §8 derives the two responses and finds them equal and opposite. That verdict is exact in the regime of the three assumptions.

Before trusting a matched induction law, name its three assumptions, write the affinity ratio the match forces, here (1+ρ)2(1+\rho)^2, and locate each circuit's inducer pair on the map.

7In the inducer total, the repressor switches where its store runs out

When the cell controls the inducer total, each circuit must first fill its own store of bound inducer. The repressor's store is its whole total, so it switches there. The activator's store is small, so it stays graded.

4 · Move a total. Let the cell set the inducer total qIq_I, as it does for a metabolite or a second messenger it makes itself. The inducer then splits between free and bound, and only the free part enters the law (18).

Counting the stored inducer at half rise gives both half-rise totals. At half rise both circuits hold free inducer KeffK_\mathrm{eff}, by eq. (18). Take the repressor first. Setting eq. (10) to the half level (2+ρ)/(2(1+ρ))(2+\rho)/(2(1+\rho)) gives R=qR/(2+ρ)R=q_R/(2+\rho). All other repressor holds an inducer, apart from at most qDq_D on the promoter, so the stored inducer is qR(1+ρ)/(2+ρ)=99.0 nMq_R(1+\rho)/(2+\rho)=99.0\ \mathrm{nM}. For the activator, the bound inducer at I=KAI/(1+ρ)I=K_{AI}/(1+\rho) is qAI/(KAI+I)=qA/(2+ρ)=0.98 nMq_AI/(K_{AI}+I)=q_A/(2+\rho)=0.98\ \mathrm{nM}. Adding free and stored inducer,

qI,1/2≈Keff+1+ρ2+ρ qR=100.0 nM  (repressor),qI,1/2≈Keff+qA2+ρ=1.99 nM  (activator).q_{I,1/2}\approx K_\mathrm{eff}+\frac{1+\rho}{2+\rho}\,q_R=100.0\ \mathrm{nM}\ \ \text{(repressor)},\qquad q_{I,1/2}\approx K_\mathrm{eff}+\frac{q_A}{2+\rho}=1.99\ \mathrm{nM}\ \ \text{(activator)}.(20)

The exact half-rise totals are 99.98 and 2.04 nM (numerical). The activator's estimate is 2.4% low, mostly because the loaded promoter also stores inducer, about 0.05 nM0.05\ \mathrm{nM} at half rise.

The shapes differ as much as the positions. In the inducer total the activator stays graded, with nH=1.02n_H=1.02, inside the cap of eq. (17). The repressor switches, with nH=25.7n_H=25.7 (both numerical).

In the tight-inducer limit the two responses are mirror images, and their Hill coefficients are related exactly. Let the inducer binding become tight, KRI→0K_{RI}\to0, with KAIK_{AI} rematched by eq. (19), and write x=qI/qRx=q_I/q_R. Then every inducer is bound. The free repressor is qR−qIq_R-q_I while x<1x<1, so eq. (10) becomes 1/(1+ρ(1−x))1/(1+\rho(1-x)), and the normalized rises of the two circuits are

NR(x)=x1+ρ(1−x),NA(x)=(1+ρ)x1+ρx,NR(x)=1−NA(1−x).N_R(x)=\frac{x}{1+\rho(1-x)},\qquad N_A(x)=\frac{(1+\rho)x}{1+\rho x},\qquad N_R(x)=1-N_A(1-x).(21)

Solving each for its 10% and 90% points gives

nR=ln⁡81ln⁡[9(1+0.1ρ)/(1+0.9ρ)]=52.2,nA=ln⁡81ln⁡[9(1+0.9ρ)/(1+0.1ρ)]=1.02,1nA+1nR=1,n_R=\frac{\ln81}{\ln\big[9(1+0.1\rho)/(1+0.9\rho)\big]}=52.2,\qquad n_A=\frac{\ln81}{\ln\big[9(1+0.9\rho)/(1+0.1\rho)\big]}=1.02,\qquad \frac1{n_A}+\frac1{n_R}=1 ,(22)

at ρ=100\rho=100, exact in the limit. For large ρ\rho, nR≈ρ/2n_R\approx\rho/2. In this limit the repressor computes a comparison of two totals, v/(aqD)≈KDR/(KDR+max⁡(0,qR−qI))v/(aq_D)\approx K_{DR}/(K_{DR}+\max(0,q_R-q_I)), the titration switch of §2 with the repressor as the sink for inducer. The activator reads the smaller of qIq_I and qAq_A through one saturating promoter.

At finite inducer affinity the steepness has a closed form, and it locates the tightness condition. With the promoter in trace, the response depends on the free inducer alone, so the 10% and 90% points in free inducer are Keff/9K_\mathrm{eff}/9 and 9Keff9K_\mathrm{eff}. The inducer total adds the stored inducer, CRI=qRI/(KRI+I)C_{RI}=q_RI/(K_{RI}+I), so ECx=Ix(1+qR/(KRI+Ix))\mathrm{EC}_x=I_x\big(1+q_R/(K_{RI}+I_x)\big). With σ=qR/KRI\sigma=q_R/K_{RI}, the ratio of the two points gives

nH=ln⁡81ln⁡ ⁣[9+9σ/(10+9ρ)1/9+σ/(10+ρ)].n_H=\frac{\ln81}{\ln\!\left[\dfrac{9+9\sigma/(10+9\rho)}{1/9+\sigma/(10+\rho)}\right]}.(23)

As σ→0\sigma\to0 the ratio is 81 and nH=1n_H=1. As σ→∞\sigma\to\infty it becomes the tight limit (22). The switch appears when the stored inducer outweighs the free inducer at both points, which needs σ≫10+9ρ\sigma\gg10+9\rho, roughly KRI≪KDR/9K_{RI}\ll K_{DR}/9: the repressor must bind its inducer sufficiently more tightly than its operator. Eq. (23) is continuous, so there is no universal threshold. At ρ=100\rho=100 and the nHn_H criterion used here, a ratio of 0.1 already gives 6.1 and a ratio of 1 gives 1.93, which is why the factor of ten is quoted as a working rule for these parameters. Eq. (23) gives 25.8, 6.11 and 1.93 at KRI/KDR=0.01K_{RI}/K_{DR}=0.01, 0.1 and 1, against exact values of 25.7, 6.10 and 1.93 with promoter loading (numerical, Figure 3).

The input must be a total the cell controls

The threshold needs two conditions: tight inducer binding, derived above, and an inducer whose total is set inside the system. A metabolite, a second messenger, a protein anti-repressor or a cell-free extract qualifies. A membrane-permeant inducer in a large medium clamps the free inducer instead, and then the effective law (18) is the right model for both circuits.

Predict a half-rise total by adding the free inducer the law needs to the inducer each regulator stores, and read from eq. (23) how steep the repressor's switch at qI≈qRq_I\approx q_R is for its affinity ratio: at qR=100KDRq_R=100K_{DR} a ratio of 0.1 gives nH≈6n_H\approx6, and the switch sharpens continuously as the ratio falls.

8The regulator and promoter totals separate the circuits again

The regulator's own total moves the repressor's threshold one for one and barely moves the activator's. The promoter total, which the effective law does not contain, separates them a third time.

The repressor's threshold tracks its own total. By eq. (20) the repressor's half-rise total is about qRq_R. Sweeping the factor's total over 50, 100 and 200 nM moves it to 49.5, 100.0 and 201.0 nM. The activator's half-rise total moves only from 3.01 to 2.04 to 1.55 nM (numerical). The activator's store, qA/(2+ρA)q_A/(2+\rho_A), stays near KDAK_{DA} whatever qAq_A is. What moves is its free-inducer half point, KAI/(1+ρA)K_{AI}/(1+\rho_A), which falls as qAq_A rises at fixed KAIK_{AI}.

In free inducer the two sensitivities to the regulator total are equal and opposite. Hold the free inducer at the half-rise point I=KeffI=K_\mathrm{eff} and change the factor's total. For the repressor, eq. (10) with R=qRKRI/(KRI+I)R=q_RK_{RI}/(K_{RI}+I) gives dln⁡v/dln⁡qR=−(R/KDR)/(1+R/KDR)d\ln v/d\ln q_R=-(R/K_{DR})/(1+R/K_{DR}), and at the half point R/KDR=ρ/(2+ρ)R/K_{DR}=\rho/(2+\rho). For the activator, the loaded fraction ϑ=c/(KDA+c)\vartheta=c/(K_{DA}+c) has dϑ/dln⁡qA=ϑ(1−ϑ)d\vartheta/d\ln q_A=\vartheta(1-\vartheta), and at the half point ϑ=ρ/(2(1+ρ))\vartheta=\rho/(2(1+\rho)). Working both through,

dln⁡vdln⁡qR=−ρ2(1+ρ),dln⁡vdln⁡qA=+ρ2(1+ρ),ρ2(1+ρ)=0.495  at ρ=100.\frac{d\ln v}{d\ln q_R}=-\frac{\rho}{2(1+\rho)},\qquad \frac{d\ln v}{d\ln q_A}=+\frac{\rho}{2(1+\rho)},\qquad \frac{\rho}{2(1+\rho)}=0.495\ \ \text{at }\rho=100 .(24)

This is exact within the reduced model, and it is Savageau's difference of response to regulatory mutations made quantitative.4

In the inducer total the repressor's sensitivity is about fifty times its free-inducer value. Holding the inducer total at each circuit's half-rise point, the sensitivity is −24.7-24.7 for the repressor, about 50 times the −0.495-0.495 of eq. (24), and +0.25+0.25 for the activator, about half its eq. (24) value (numerical). The two circuits now differ about a hundredfold in size of sensitivity. Near its threshold the repressor turns a 1% change in its own total into about a 25% change in output. This is a static sensitivity: it predicts how a change of the factor's total slower than 1/δ1/\delta shows up in the output. No noise was simulated.

The promoter total separates the circuits a third time. Raise qDq_D past the factor's total. With tight promoter binding, an uninduced repressor occupies one site each, so the free promoter is about max⁡(0,qD−qR)\max(0,q_D-q_R) and the production per promoter about (qD−qR)/qD(q_D-q_R)/q_D once qD>qRq_D>q_R. With saturating inducer, the activator loads one site each, so the loaded promoter is about min⁡(qD,qA)\min(q_D,q_A) and the production per promoter is about a0/a+(a1−a0)/a⋅min⁡(1,qA/qD)a_0/a+(a_1-a_0)/a\cdot\min(1,q_A/q_D). Both estimates give 0.50 at qD=200 nMq_D=200\ \mathrm{nM}, against exact values of 0.505 (numerical). At 1000 nM the repressor circuit reaches 0.90 and the activator circuit falls to 0.11. The effective law (18) contains no qDq_D, so it predicts a production per promoter independent of copy number in both.

Measurement

Brewster and colleagues measured the repressor side of this result for the Lac repressor in E. coli, with the repressed gene on multicopy plasmids or at five chromosomal sites. The measured fold-change in expression stayed near 1 whenever repressors were fewer than gene copies, as the caption of their Figure 4 states (p. 1316).5

Use the regulator total and the promoter total as two further inputs: in free inducer the sensitivities to the regulator total are ∓ρ/(2(1+ρ))\mp\rho/(2(1+\rho)), and in the inducer total a repressor near its threshold amplifies changes in its own total many fold.

9Closing the inducer loop: removal decides what the steady state reads

Closing the output loop adds nothing while the inducer total is fixed. Once the inducer is made and removed, the removal rule decides whether the steady state reads the free inducer or the total.

5 · Close the loop. With the inducer total fixed, the output obeys q˙G=v−δqG\dot q_G=v-\delta q_G, which filters v with the same time 1/δ1/\delta in both circuits. Closing that loop changes no comparison. Let the inducer total itself be dynamic, supplied by ∅⇝I\varnothing\rightsquigarrow I with rate law u, and dilute the output at δ=λ\delta=\lambda. Time is in units of 1/λ1/\lambda.

If only free inducer is removed, both circuits reach the same steady state, at different times. The inducer obeys q˙I=u−δII\dot q_I=u-\delta_II, so at steady state I∗=u/δII^*=u/\delta_I exactly, whatever the binding. Both circuits settle at the output the free-inducer law (18) gives, 0.505 when I∗=KeffI^*=K_\mathrm{eff}, that is at u=0.101 λqRu=0.101\,\lambda q_R with δI=10λ\delta_I=10\lambda. The repressor must first fill a store of about qRq_R, which takes about qR/u≈10/λq_R/u\approx10/\lambda. It reaches half its final output at λt=10.6\lambda t=10.6, against 0.85 for the activator (numerical). Binding protects the stored inducer from removal.

If every inducer-containing state is diluted, the steady state reads the total. Uniform dilution gives q˙I=u−λqI\dot q_I=u-\lambda q_I, so

qI(t)=uλ(1−e−λt)q_I(t)=\frac{u}{\lambda}\big(1-e^{-\lambda t}\big)(25)

in both circuits, exactly, whatever the binding. At the same supply the steady total is 10.1 nM, and the activator reaches 0.84 while the repressor stays at 0.011 (numerical). The repressor turns on only when the steady total passes its half-rise total, about qR+Keffq_R+K_\mathrm{eff}, that is when u>λ(qR+Keff)u>\lambda(q_R+K_\mathrm{eff}). At u=2λqRu=2\lambda q_R, eq. (25) crosses qRq_R when e−λt=1/2e^{-\lambda t}=1/2, at λt=ln⁡2\lambda t=\ln2, and the production per promoter switches there. The output protein follows through its own removal filter, with time 1/δ1/\delta. The repressor total is itself held by synthesis at λqR\lambda q_R, so the threshold sits where the two synthesis rates match, the in vivo titration threshold of Buchler and Louis (pp. 1106 to 1110).6

Close an inducer loop with a named removal rule: removal of free inducer only makes the steady state read the free inducer and delays the repressor by about qR/uq_R/u, while uniform dilution makes it read the total and switches the repressor where the inducer supply passes λqR\lambda q_R.

Part 3

Ultrasensitivity

A threshold from two saturated enzymes, and a threshold from one tight binding layer whose input is a total. In both, the threshold sits at a total. The core shows the finite-pool picture.

10The modification cycle with every complex kept

The canonical switch is a covalent-modification cycle. Written with both enzyme complexes kept in the substrate total, it is two binding pairs and one slow balance with exactly one stable steady state.

Two measures of steepness are used, and a threshold is a claim about the second. The Hill coefficient nH=ln⁡81/ln⁡(EC90/EC10)n_H=\ln81/\ln(\mathrm{EC}_{90}/\mathrm{EC}_{10}) of §5 summarizes the whole rise from 10% to 90%. The local order dln⁡(output)/dln⁡(input)d\ln(\text{output})/d\ln(\text{input}) is the slope on log axes at one point, Lecture 8's gain. A hard saturation corner can raise nHn_H without any point of high local order, so a threshold is checked with the local order.

1 · Model. A kinase E converts the substrate X into its modified form Y, and a phosphatase F converts it back. Each enzyme binds its substrate form in an elementary step and acts in a composite catalytic step, with co-substrates held fixed and the reverse activity neglected:

E+X⇌k−Ek+ECEX,CEX⇝E+Y  (rate law kECEX),F+Y⇌k−Fk+FCFY,CFY⇝F+X  (rate law kFCFY).\begin{aligned}&E+X\xrightleftharpoons[k_{-E}]{k_{+E}}C_{EX},\qquad C_{EX}\rightsquigarrow E+Y\ \ (\text{rate law }k_EC_{EX}),\\ &F+Y\xrightleftharpoons[k_{-F}]{k_{+F}}C_{FY},\qquad C_{FY}\rightsquigarrow F+X\ \ (\text{rate law }k_FC_{FY}).\end{aligned}(26)

The totals are qE=E+CEXq_E=E+C_{EX}, qF=F+CFYq_F=F+C_{FY} and the substrate total qS=X+Y+CEX+CFYq_S=X+Y+C_{EX}+C_{FY}, which the cycle conserves. The modified total, free or bound to the phosphatase, is qY=Y+CFYq_Y=Y+C_{FY}, and the unmodified total is qS−qY=X+CEXq_S-q_Y=X+C_{EX}.

Each enzyme forms one pair with its own substrate form, so eq. (4) gives both complexes. The kinase pairs with the unmodified total and the phosphatase with the modified total: CEX=C(qE,qS−qY;KE)C_{EX}=C(q_E,q_S-q_Y;K_E) and CFY=C(qF,qY;KF)C_{FY}=C(q_F,q_Y;K_F), where C(⋅)C(\cdot) is the root (4) and KEK_E, KFK_F are the two dissociation constants. The slow variable obeys

q˙Y=kE C(qE,qS−qY;KE)−kF C(qF,qY;KF).\dot q_Y=k_E\,C(q_E,q_S-q_Y;K_E)-k_F\,C(q_F,q_Y;K_F).(27)

The root (4) rises with each of its totals. So the first term falls and the second rises as qYq_Y grows, and eq. (27) has exactly one steady state, which is stable. The cycle cannot hold two states by itself.

The experiment varies the ratio of the enzyme totals. The input is r=qE/qFr=q_E/q_F with equal catalytic constants, kE=kFk_E=k_F, so r is the ratio of the two maximal rates. The readout is the modified fraction y=qY/qSy=q_Y/q_S. Both enzymes share one dissociation constant K, which is also their Michaelis constant when catalysis is slow against unbinding.

Write a modification cycle as two binding pairs plus the slow balance (27), and conclude from monotonicity alone that it has one stable steady state at every input.

11Saturation is the route to steepness, and a large phosphatase share caps it

In this cycle the steepness comes from saturating both enzymes. One saturated enzyme gives at most nH=2n_H=2. For the modified fraction read against the enzyme ratio, a phosphatase holding more than a small share of the substrate caps the steepness however saturated the enzymes are.

2 · Limit. Goldbeter and Koshland took both enzymes in trace, so that the complexes are negligible in the substrate total and each free substrate form wins its own total.7 Each complex then follows eq. (5). With Kˉ=K/qS\bar K=K/q_S, setting eq. (27) to zero gives their closed form:

r=y (Kˉ+1−y)(1−y)(Kˉ+y),RV=r(0.9)r(0.1)=81(Kˉ+0.1)2(Kˉ+0.9)2,nH=ln⁡81ln⁡RV.r=\frac{y\,(\bar K+1-y)}{(1-y)(\bar K+y)},\qquad R_V=\frac{r(0.9)}{r(0.1)}=\frac{81(\bar K+0.1)^2}{(\bar K+0.9)^2},\qquad n_H=\frac{\ln81}{\ln R_V}.(28)

These are their Eqs. 7 to 10 (pp. 6841 to 6842) with equal constants for the two enzymes. 3 · Match. In the trace limit the exact cycle (27) reproduces eq. (28) to 6×10−66\times10^{-6} (numerical).

Saturation sets the steepness. For a saturating substrate, Kˉ≪1\bar K\ll1, expand the logarithm. Since ln⁡81+2ln⁡(0.1/0.9)=0\ln81+2\ln(0.1/0.9)=0, only the first-order terms survive: ln⁡RV≈2Kˉ(10−10/9)=(160/9)Kˉ\ln R_V\approx2\bar K(10-10/9)=(160/9)\bar K. Therefore

nH≈9ln⁡81160 qSK=0.247 qSK.n_H\approx\frac{9\ln81}{160}\,\frac{q_S}{K}=0.247\,\frac{q_S}{K}.(29)

At qS=100Kq_S=100K the rise from 10% to 90% spans r from 0.919 to 1.088, an 18% change of the enzyme ratio. At qS=Kq_S=K the switch is barely there, nH=1.33n_H=1.33 (both from eq. 28).

One saturated enzyme gives at most 2, so a sharper switch needs both. Let the phosphatase work in its first-order range, KˉF→∞\bar K_F\to\infty, in the two-constant form of Eq. 10. The response ratio becomes RV=81(KˉE+0.1)/(KˉE+0.9)R_V=81(\bar K_E+0.1)/(\bar K_E+0.9), which falls to 9 as the kinase saturates, so nH→2n_H\to2 and stops (exact). Goldbeter and Koshland's condition is that "one or more" of the enzymes work in the zero-order region (p. 6840). One saturated enzyme already makes the response ultrasensitive, up to 2. A switch steeper than that needs both. Saturation is the route to steepness in this cycle. It is not the only route in general, and §13 reaches a threshold through sequestration instead.

4 · Move a total. An abundant phosphatase caps the switch, because it holds the modified substrate. Raise the phosphatase total to a fraction f=qF/qSf=q_F/q_S of the substrate and take binding tight. In that limit each complex is the smaller of its two totals, and flux balance at equal catalytic constants sets CEX=CFYC_{EX}=C_{FY}. There are two cases, f<1/2f<1/2 and f≥1/2f\ge1/2. Take f<1/2f<1/2 first. Below the balance point r=1r=1 the phosphatase out-runs the kinase, so every modified substrate sits on the phosphatase: CFY=qEC_{FY}=q_E, and y=rfy=rf. Above it the phosphatase is full, CFY=qFC_{FY}=q_F, the kinase holds the whole unmodified total qFq_F, and y=1−fy=1-f. The normalized rise reaches 10% at r=0.1(1−f)/fr=0.1(1-f)/f on the linear part. It reaches 90% on the linear part only if 0.9(1−f)≤f0.9(1-f)\le f, and otherwise at the jump, r=1r=1.

For f≥1/2f\ge1/2 the phosphatase can never be filled, because the plateau 1−f1-f would leave it less modified substrate than its own total. Once the kinase total passes half the substrate, at r=1/(2f)r=1/(2f), each enzyme holds the whole of its substrate form, and CEX=CFYC_{EX}=C_{FY} forces y=1/2y=1/2. The response is y=rfy=rf up to r=1/(2f)r=1/(2f) and then the plateau 1/21/2, with no jump at r=1r=1. At qS=1q_S=1, f=0.8f=0.8, r=100r=100 and K=10−8qSK=10^{-8}q_S the exact cycle gives y=0.5000000083y=0.5000000083 (numerical). Normalized by its plateau the rise is linear from start to end, so nH=ln⁡81/ln⁡9=2n_H=\ln81/\ln9=2. The two cases combine into

nHmax=ln⁡81ln⁡(10f/(1−f))for 111<f<919,nHmax=2for f≥919,n_H^\mathrm{max}=\frac{\ln81}{\ln\big(10f/(1-f)\big)}\quad\text{for}\ \tfrac1{11}<f<\tfrac9{19},\qquad n_H^\mathrm{max}=2\quad\text{for}\ f\ge\tfrac9{19},(30)

with the plateau 1−f1-f below f=1/2f=1/2 and 1/21/2 above it. The cap is 41.7 at f=0.1f=0.1 and 3.0 at f=0.3f=0.3. Unbounded steepness of this readout needs f≤1/11f\le1/11, a phosphatase scarcer than qS/11q_S/11. That condition is exact in the tight limit for this normalized readout, the total modified fraction against the ratio of enzyme totals. It is not a requirement for steepness in general, and not a necessary condition for every catalytic switch. The exact cycle approaches these caps as the substrate saturates (numerical, Figure 4). Goldbeter and Koshland remarked that enzyme ratios of 0.1 or less change little at their parameters (p. 6842). That agrees, because at qS/K=10q_S/K=10 the cap of 42 is far above the trace value of 3.7.

5 · Close the loop. The cycle has one stable state at every input, by §10, so its steepness is a static input-output behavior: the steady state as a function of the enzyme ratio. It is not an autonomous dynamical behavior such as memory or a cycle. A steep static response becomes one only when a loop feeds the output back, which Part 4 does with a titration layer instead.

Read a catalytic switch's steepness from eq. (29), about 0.25 qS/K0.25\,q_S/K, with both enzymes saturated, since one alone gives at most nH=2n_H=2. For the modified fraction against the enzyme ratio, read the cap of eq. (30) from the phosphatase share: unbounded only below f=1/11f=1/11, and 2 from f=9/19f=9/19 on.

12In free ligand, negative cooperativity flattens

A receptor with two sites, only the doubly bound state active, can make a threshold with one binding layer. Measured against free ligand, though, negative cooperativity makes its response flatter, not steeper.

1 · Model. A receptor R binds ligand L at two identical sites, first with the site constant K1K_1 and then, with one site filled, with K2K_2. An empty receptor offers two sites, so its association runs at 2k+1RL2k_{+1}RL. A doubly bound receptor can lose either ligand, so its dissociation runs at 2k−2CRL22k_{-2}C_{RL_2}. Writing those factors into the elementary arrows,

R+L⇌k−12k+1CRL,CRL+L⇌2k−2k+2CRL2,K1=k−1k+1,K2=k−2k+2.R+L\xrightleftharpoons[k_{-1}]{2k_{+1}}C_{RL},\qquad C_{RL}+L\xrightleftharpoons[2k_{-2}]{k_{+2}}C_{RL_2},\qquad K_1=\frac{k_{-1}}{k_{+1}},\quad K_2=\frac{k_{-2}}{k_{+2}}.(31)

Equilibrium of each step then gives

CRL=2RLK1,CRL2=CRLL2K2=RL2K1K2,C_{RL}=\frac{2RL}{K_1},\qquad C_{RL_2}=\frac{C_{RL}L}{2K_2}=\frac{RL^2}{K_1K_2},(32)

with totals qR=R+CRL+CRL2q_R=R+C_{RL}+C_{RL_2} and qL=L+CRL+2CRL2q_L=L+C_{RL}+2C_{RL_2}. The cooperativity is c=K1/K2c=K_1/K_2. It is negative when c<1c<1, so that the second ligand binds more weakly than the first. The observable is the active fraction CRL2/qRC_{RL_2}/q_R. The illustrative constants are K1=10−4 μMK_1=10^{-4}\ \mu\mathrm M and K2=10−2 μMK_2=10^{-2}\ \mu\mathrm M, so c=0.01c=0.01.

The exact equilibrium is one monotone equation for the free ligand. Substituting eq. (32) into the ligand total,

L+qR 2L/K1+2L2/(K1K2)1+2L/K1+L2/(K1K2)=qL.L+q_R\,\frac{2L/K_1+2L^2/(K_1K_2)}{1+2L/K_1+L^2/(K_1K_2)}=q_L .(33)

The left side rises strictly with L, so there is one root, and every species follows from it.

2 · Limit. The classical treatment takes the ligand in excess, so that the free ligand equals its total. The fast subsystem removed is the binding layer, and the dominance choice is that free ligand wins its own total. The active fraction is then a function of free ligand alone:

CRL2qR=L2/(K1K2)1+2L/K1+L2/(K1K2).\frac{C_{RL_2}}{q_R}=\frac{L^2/(K_1K_2)}{1+2L/K_1+L^2/(K_1K_2)}.(34)

Its Hill coefficient lies between 1 and 2. For strong negative cooperativity, once L≫K1L\gg K_1 the first site is full and eq. (34) becomes L/(2K2+L)L/(2K_2+L), a Michaelis-Menten law, so nH→1n_H\to1. For strong positive cooperativity it becomes L2/(K1K2+L2)L^2/(K_1K_2+L^2), so nH→2n_H\to2. The computed values are 1.000 at c=10−4c=10^{-4}, 1.005 at c=0.01c=0.01, 1.19 at c=1c=1 and 1.98 at c=104c=10^4 (numerical, from eq. 34). Ha and Ferrell describe the same trend (p. 990).8

3 · Match. Eq. (34) is exact when the receptor cannot deplete the ligand, that is when qR≪K2q_R\ll K_2. There the response to the ligand total rises half-way near qL=2K2q_L=2K_2, with nH=1.02n_H=1.02 at qR=10−4 μMq_R=10^{-4}\ \mu\mathrm M (numerical), as the free-ligand law does.

Write a multisite receptor with its statistical factors in the elementary arrows, solve it by the monotone equation (33), and expect a free-ligand response with nHn_H between 1 and 2 that negative cooperativity pushes toward 1.

13In the ligand total, the first sites buffer the input

When the receptor total exceeds its second dissociation constant and the input is the ligand total, the singly bound receptors absorb the first ligands one each. The response stays flat up to the receptor total and then rises straight to full.

4 · Move a total. Raise the receptor total past K2K_2, to qR=1 μMq_R=1\ \mu\mathrm M, and sweep the ligand total. Count before computing. The first site binds a hundred times more tightly than the second, so the first ligands go to empty receptors. Until qLq_L reaches qRq_R, nearly every receptor holds at most one ligand, and the active state stays empty. Past that point the two totals read CRL+CRL2≈qRC_{RL}+C_{RL_2}\approx q_R and CRL+2CRL2≈qLC_{RL}+2C_{RL_2}\approx q_L, because nearly every receptor and every ligand is bound. Subtracting,

CRL2qR≈qLqR−1for  qR<qL<2qR.\frac{C_{RL_2}}{q_R}\approx\frac{q_L}{q_R}-1\qquad\text{for}\ \ q_R<q_L<2q_R .(35)

The rise from 10% to 90% then spans qL/qRq_L/q_R from 1.1 to 1.9, which gives nH=ln⁡81/ln⁡(1.9/1.1)=8.04n_H=\ln81/\ln(1.9/1.1)=8.04, exact in the limit. This is the maximum Ha and Ferrell found as c→0c\to0 (p. 991). At the illustrative constants the exact response has nH=6.73n_H=6.73, with 10%, 50% and 90% points at 1.08, 1.52 and 2.08 μM and a local order of 11.0 near qL≈qRq_L\approx q_R. The same receptor has nH=1.005n_H=1.005 in free ligand (both numerical).

The threshold needs two separate conditions. Negative cooperativity, c≪1c\ll1, makes the singly bound receptors a buffer that absorbs the first qRq_R of ligand. Tight binding, K2≪qRK_2\ll q_R, makes the ligand total the effective input. Without negative cooperativity, at c=1c=1, the two sites fill independently. With all ligand bound, each site is occupied with probability qL/(2qR)q_L/(2q_R), so the active fraction is (qL/2qR)2(q_L/2q_R)^2, with local order exactly 2. Its 10% and 90% points are 20.1 qR2\sqrt{0.1}\,q_R and 20.9 qR2\sqrt{0.9}\,q_R, so nH=ln⁡81/ln⁡3=4n_H=\ln81/\ln3=4. That high value comes from the depletion corner at 2qR2q_R, not from a threshold. With a weak second site, K2=qRK_2=q_R, the response stays near nH=1.6n_H=1.6 (numerical).

Measurement

Ha and Ferrell built the two-site receptor from DNA strands and held it at 1000 nM (p. 991). From their threshold data they inferred c=0.022±0.014c=0.022\pm0.014 for one ligand pair (supplement, Table S1), near the illustrative 0.01.8 In budding yeast, Buchler and Cross measured apparent Hill coefficients up to 12 from a transcription factor sequestered by an inhibitor, with threshold and steepness set by the inhibitor's abundance (p. 1).9

Get a threshold from one binding layer by making the input a total, with a buffer that binds first (c≪1c\ll1) and binding tight against the partner total (K2≪qRK_2\ll q_R): the response is flat to qL=qRq_L=q_R and then follows eq. (35).

14The threshold sits at a total, so a fitted Hill function cannot travel

The receptor's threshold is its own total. A Hill function fitted at one receptor total stores the threshold as a constant, so it misses as soon as that total moves.

The half-rise point moves from 2K22K_2 to 1.5qR1.5q_R as the receptor total grows. While qR≪K2q_R\ll K_2 the free-ligand law (34) holds and the half-rise is near 2K22K_2. Once qR≫K2q_R\gg K_2, eq. (35) puts it at 1.5qR1.5q_R. Along the way the Hill coefficient rises from 1.02 at qR=10−4 μMq_R=10^{-4}\ \mu\mathrm M through 3.6 at 0.1 μM0.1\ \mu\mathrm M to 7.8 at 100 μM100\ \mu\mathrm M (numerical).

A Hill function fitted at one receptor total misses at the next. The Hill function through the exact 10% and 90% points at qR=1 μMq_R=1\ \mu\mathrm M has half-rise KH=1.50 μMK_H=1.50\ \mu\mathrm M and coefficient 6.73. At qR=0.3q_R=0.3 and 3 μM3\ \mu\mathrm M the exact half-rise points are 0.47 and 4.52 μM, so the fit misses them 3.2-fold and 3.0-fold, and the exact coefficients change to 5.28 and 7.39 (numerical). The fit stores the threshold as a constant. The mechanism places it at a total.

At fixed ligand the active receptor rises and then falls with the receptor total. Apply the same counts with the roles swapped, holding qLq_L and sweeping qRq_R. While qR<qL/2q_R<q_L/2 there is ligand for every site, and CRL2≈qRC_{RL_2}\approx q_R. Between qL/2q_L/2 and qLq_L, eq. (35) gives CRL2≈qL−qRC_{RL_2}\approx q_L-q_R, because added receptors take ligand one at a time and complete fewer pairs. So the active receptor peaks at qR=qL/2q_R=q_L/2: at 0.100 μM for qL=0.2 μMq_L=0.2\ \mu\mathrm M (numerical). A model without ligand depletion keeps rising. Ha and Ferrell predicted and measured this peak, at a receptor-to-ligand ratio of 1:2 (p. 993).8

5 · Close the loop. A threshold becomes a behavior only inside a loop. Parts 4 and 6 put the same mechanism, a pool whose total sets a threshold, into feedback loops: a finite promoter pool read by monomeric repressors. The repressor of §7 is the same mechanism once more, with the repressor as the sink for inducer. Buchler and Louis state the pair of controls for such titration: the titrant total sets the threshold's position, and the ratio of that total to KdK_d sets its sharpness (pp. 1108 to 1109).6

Refit a Hill function whenever the partner total moves, or better, place the threshold at the partner total: half-rise near 1.5qR1.5q_R for the two-site receptor, and a peak at qR=qL/2q_R=q_L/2 when the receptor total is swept.

Part 4

Multistability

Memory needs several stable states of the closed loop. Two comparisons follow: the same toggle mechanism in two limits, and two architectures for N factors. The core shows the circuits and their time courses.

15The Hill toggle needs the product of its coefficients above one

The effective model of mutual repression is the Hill toggle. It holds a single stable state whenever the product of its two Hill coefficients is at most one, and a short index argument proves it.

1 · Effective model. Gardner, Cantor and Collins wrote the toggle in dimensionless form (Box 1, p. 339):10

u˙=α11+vβ−u,v˙=α21+uγ−v.\dot u=\frac{\alpha_1}{1+v^{\beta}}-u,\qquad \dot v=\frac{\alpha_2}{1+u^{\gamma}}-v .(36)

Here u and v are the two repressor totals in units of the repression constant, time is in removal lifetimes, α1\alpha_1 and α2\alpha_2 are synthesis strengths, and β\beta and γ\gamma are Hill coefficients. These letters are the authors' and hold only in this section. Every arrow is composite: ∅⇝R1\varnothing\rightsquigarrow R_1 with rate law α1/(1+vβ)\alpha_1/(1+v^\beta), and removal with rate law u. Nothing in eq. (36) resolves binding, so each exponent is a fitted cooperativity. Gardner and colleagues attribute it to multimerization and cooperative binding to several operator sites.

One stable state without cooperativity

If βγ≤1\beta\gamma\le1, the toggle (36) has exactly one fixed point for every α1,α2>0\alpha_1,\alpha_2>0, and every trajectory converges to it.

The proof has three steps: every fixed point is a stable node, there is exactly one, and no cycle exists. Write f1(v)=α1/(1+vβ)f_1(v)=\alpha_1/(1+v^\beta) and f2(u)=α2/(1+uγ)f_2(u)=\alpha_2/(1+u^\gamma). At a fixed point u=f1(v)u=f_1(v), so f1′(v)=−(u/v) e1f_1'(v)=-(u/v)\,e_1 with e1=βvβ/(1+vβ)<βe_1=\beta v^\beta/(1+v^\beta)<\beta, the log-slope of the first repression law. Likewise f2′(u)=−(v/u) e2f_2'(u)=-(v/u)\,e_2 with e2=γuγ/(1+uγ)<γe_2=\gamma u^\gamma/(1+u^\gamma)<\gamma. The Jacobian (−1f1′f2′−1)\begin{pmatrix}-1&f_1'\\f_2'&-1\end{pmatrix} has trace −2-2 and determinant 1−e1e2>1−βγ≥01-e_1e_2>1-\beta\gamma\ge0, so every fixed point is a stable node, of index +1. On the boundary of the box [0,α1+1]×[0,α2+1][0,\alpha_1+1]\times[0,\alpha_2+1] the field points strictly inward, so the indices inside sum to +1, and there is exactly one fixed point. The divergence is −2-2 everywhere, so Bendixson's criterion excludes periodic orbits, and the Poincaré-Bendixson theorem sends every trajectory to the fixed point.

The converse holds: a product above one opens a bistable wedge. The saddle-node set is e1e2=1e_1e_2=1, which needs βγ>1\beta\gamma>1. On the diagonal, with β=γ=n\beta=\gamma=n and α1=α2=α\alpha_1=\alpha_2=\alpha, the symmetric state x=α/(1+xn)x=\alpha/(1+x^n) splits when its log-slope reaches 1, at xn=1/(n−1)x^n=1/(n-1). So the symmetric threshold is

αc(n)=nn−1 (n−1)−1/n,\alpha_c(n)=\frac{n}{n-1}\,(n-1)^{-1/n},(37)

which is 2 at n=2n=2, 1.19 at n=3n=3 and 89.2 at n=1.1n=1.1 (exact). On a grid of 1681 synthesis pairs from 0.1 to 1000, no point is bistable at n=0.8n=0.8 or 1, and 11, 339 and 536 points are bistable at n=1.1n=1.1, 2 and 3 (numerical).

Cherry and Adler stated the condition for any two repression laws. With P(f)=sup⁡y[−yf′(y)/f(y)]P(f)=\sup_y[-yf'(y)/f(y)], the largest log-slope, multiple equilibria need P(f)P(g)≥1P(f)P(g)\ge1, and some removal rates give them when P(f)P(g)>1P(f)P(g)>1 (Proposition 1.1, p. 123).11 For a Hill law P=nP=n. Gardner and colleagues state the weaker form, that at least one repressor must act with cooperativity greater than one (p. 339).

Before expecting a Hill toggle to hold two states, check the product of its two Hill coefficients: at most one means one globally attracting state, and above one opens a bistable wedge whose symmetric edge is eq. (37).

16A finite promoter pool makes a monomeric toggle bistable

The same monomeric toggle, written with its promoter sites, is monostable in its trace-promoter limit and bistable once the site pool exceeds the dissociation constant. This is the strict comparison of one mechanism with its own effective law.

1 · Model. Repressor R2R_2 binds the promoter sites P1P_1 of gene 1 as a monomer, one repressor per site, and only free sites express R1R_1. Every site also leaks at a small rate. Free and bound repressor are diluted alike, the uniform variant θ=1\theta=1:

R2+P1⇌k−k+CP1R2,P1⇝P1+R1  (rate law (kP+kℓ)P1),CP1R2⇝CP1R2+R1  (rate law kℓCP1R2),R2⇝∅  (rate law λR2),CP1R2⇝P1  (rate law λCP1R2),\begin{aligned}&R_2+P_1\xrightleftharpoons[k_-]{k_+}C_{P_1R_2},\\ &P_1\rightsquigarrow P_1+R_1\ \ (\text{rate law }(k_P+k_\ell)P_1),\qquad C_{P_1R_2}\rightsquigarrow C_{P_1R_2}+R_1\ \ (\text{rate law }k_\ell C_{P_1R_2}),\\ &R_2\rightsquigarrow\varnothing\ \ (\text{rate law }\lambda R_2),\qquad C_{P_1R_2}\rightsquigarrow P_1\ \ (\text{rate law }\lambda C_{P_1R_2}),\end{aligned}(38)

and symmetrically for gene 2. Here K=k−/k+K=k_-/k_+ is the dissociation constant of one repressor and one site, qPq_P is the site total of each gene, kPk_P the production per free site and kℓk_\ell the leak per site, free or bound. The two production steps sum to kPP1+kℓqPk_PP_1+k_\ell q_P. The last step is growth dilution of a bound repressor: growth copies the genes, so the site total qPq_P stays fixed while the repressor on a site is diluted, and the site reappears free. Because free and bound repressor leave at the same rate, the total balance q˙R1=kPP1+kℓqP−λqR1\dot q_{R_1}=k_PP_1+k_\ell q_P-\lambda q_{R_1} is exact. Only the binding layer uses fast equilibrium.

The free fraction of sites solves a quadratic. Measure the repressor total and the dissociation constant in units of the pool: r=qR/qPr=q_R/q_P and κ=K/qP\kappa=K/q_P. With p=P/qPp=P/q_P the free fraction, the bound sites are 1−p1-p and the free repressor is r−(1−p)r-(1-p), in units of qPq_P. Equilibrium, P⋅R=K CP\cdot R=K\,C, becomes p (r−1+p)=κ(1−p)p\,(r-1+p)=\kappa(1-p), whose physical root and inverse are

p(r)=12[(r−1+κ)2+4κ−(r−1+κ)],r(p)=(1−p)(p+κ)p.p(r)=\tfrac12\Big[\sqrt{(r-1+\kappa)^2+4\kappa}-(r-1+\kappa)\Big],\qquad r(p)=\frac{(1-p)(p+\kappa)}{p}.(39)

Below equivalence the free fraction falls linearly, and above it collapses. Take tight binding, κ≪1\kappa\ll1. Below equivalence, where 1−r≫κ1-r\gg\sqrt\kappa, each repressor occupies one site, so p≈1−rp\approx1-r: the free promoter falls in proportion, while the free repressor stays tiny, about κr/(1−r)\kappa r/(1-r). Past equivalence, where r−1≫κr-1\gg\sqrt\kappa, the sites are full and every further repressor stays free, so p≈κ/(r−1)p\approx\kappa/(r-1). At equivalence, r=1r=1, the quadratic gives p2=κ(1−p)p^2=\kappa(1-p), so p≈κp\approx\sqrt\kappa. That is the small free pool KqP\sqrt{Kq_P} on the singular ray of §2. Each asymptotic piece holds only on its own side, and the exact quadratic (39) bridges the corner ∣r−1∣≲κ|r-1|\lesssim\sqrt\kappa.

The log-slope of the free fraction measures how sharply the pool switches. Differentiating r(p)r(p) gives dr/dp=−(p2+κ)/p2dr/dp=-(p^2+\kappa)/p^2, so

−dln⁡pdln⁡r=r pp2+κ.-\frac{d\ln p}{d\ln r}=\frac{r\,p}{p^2+\kappa}.(40)

In the limit κ→0\kappa\to0 below equivalence, p=1−rp=1-r and the log-slope is r/(1−r)r/(1-r), which exceeds 1 for r>1/2r>1/2 and grows without bound as r→1r\to1. A straight fall on linear axes is a steep fall on log axes. At finite κ\kappa the peak has a closed form. Differentiating eq. (40) written in p, r(p)p/(p2+κ)=(1−p)(p+κ)/(p2+κ)r(p)p/(p^2+\kappa)=(1-p)(p+\kappa)/(p^2+\kappa), and setting the derivative to zero gives

ppeak=κ 1−κ1+κ,rpeak=(1+κ)21−κ,(−dln⁡pdln⁡r)max⁡=1+κ2κ.p_\mathrm{peak}=\sqrt\kappa\,\frac{1-\sqrt\kappa}{1+\sqrt\kappa},\qquad r_\mathrm{peak}=\frac{(1+\kappa)^2}{1-\kappa},\qquad \Big(-\frac{d\ln p}{d\ln r}\Big)_{\max}=\frac{1+\kappa}{2\sqrt\kappa}.(40a)

These hold for 0<κ<10<\kappa<1, that is qP>Kq_P>K. For κ≥1\kappa\ge1 the formula for ppeakp_\mathrm{peak} gives no physical fraction, and there is no interior peak: the log-slope rises with r toward 1 and never reaches it. At κ=0.005\kappa=0.005 the peak is 7.106423 at r=1.015101r=1.015101, while at equivalence itself the slope is 7.066653 (exact). Both share the leading term 12qP/K\tfrac12\sqrt{q_P/K}, which is 7.07 here, so the two agree to within 0.6% (Figure 6).

In units of the pool and the dilution time, the toggle is two equations. With a=kP/λa=k_P/\lambda, the repressors one free site makes per lifetime, and ε=kℓ/kP\varepsilon=k_\ell/k_P, the leak,

r˙1=a(p(r2)+ε)−r1,r˙2=a(p(r1)+ε)−r2.\dot r_1=a\big(p(r_2)+\varepsilon\big)-r_1,\qquad \dot r_2=a\big(p(r_1)+\varepsilon\big)-r_2 .(41)

2 · Limit. Put the promoter in trace, qP≪Kq_P\ll K. The repressor then wins its own total, the free repressor equals the total, and p=κ/(κ+r)=K/(K+qR)p=\kappa/(\kappa+r)=K/(K+q_R), a Hill law of coefficient 1 in the repressor total. The fast subsystem removed is the binding layer, and the dominance choice is a promoter in trace. Eq. (41) becomes the toggle (36) with β=γ=1\beta=\gamma=1. 3 · Match. In this limit the two models are the same equations, and by §15 they hold exactly one stable state.

4 · Move a total. Raise the pool above K. The symmetric state, without leak, has r∗=ap∗r^*=ap^*. The gain of each link, the slope with which one node's production answers its upstream total relative to its removal slope of 1, is H=a ∣p′(r∗)∣=ap∗2/(p∗2+κ)H=a\,|p'(r^*)|=ap^{*2}/(p^{*2}+\kappa). Using a=r∗/p∗a=r^*/p^* and eq. (39),

H=(1−p∗)(p∗+κ)p∗2+κ.H=\frac{(1-p^*)(p^*+\kappa)}{p^{*2}+\kappa}.(42)

The Jacobian at the symmetric state is (−1−H−H−1)\begin{pmatrix}-1&-H\\-H&-1\end{pmatrix}, with eigenvalues −1±H-1\pm H. So the symmetric state is a saddle exactly when H>1H>1, where the loop gain H2H^2 of the two links passes 1. Clearing the denominator, H>1H>1 becomes p∗(1−κ−2p∗)>0p^*(1-\kappa-2p^*)>0, that is p∗<(1−κ)/2p^*<(1-\kappa)/2, which needs κ<1\kappa<1. Since a=(1−p)(p+κ)/p2a=(1-p)(p+\kappa)/p^2 falls as p rises, the condition on the production is a>a((1−κ)/2)a>a\big((1-\kappa)/2\big):

qP>Kanda>(1+κ1−κ)2.q_P>K\qquad\text{and}\qquad a>\Big(\frac{1+\kappa}{1-\kappa}\Big)^{2}.(43)

So monomeric repressors make a toggle once the site pool exceeds the dissociation constant and production is high enough (exact for the symmetric state). The number of stable states, computed on 36 grid points with κ\kappa from 0.01 to 2 and a from 1.5 to 1000, matches eq. (43) at every point (numerical).

5 · Close the loop. The removal rule matters here too. If bound repressor is protected, the gain becomes 1−p∗<11-p^*<1, and §27 proves that the toggle then holds one state for every parameter. Cherry and Adler showed that depletion of free repressor can make a switch without cooperative binding, given more than one operator copy per cell, a small enough dissociation constant, and equal decay of free and bound repressor (pp. 127 to 128). Their pool condition is that the operator total exceed the dissociation constant.11 Eq. (43) adds the production threshold, in closed form.

Decide whether monomeric repressors can make a toggle from the pool and the production: the trace-promoter limit never can, and a finite pool can exactly when qP>Kq_P>K and a>((1+κ)/(1−κ))2a>((1+\kappa)/(1-\kappa))^2, with bound repressor removed alongside free.

17N Hill genes keep at most one node raised

Generalized to N mutually repressing genes, the Hill toggle keeps at most one node high in any stable state. That part is a theorem. The resulting count of N + 1 states holds over the parameter grid searched.

1 · Effective model. Each of N genes is repressed by all the others through a product of Hill laws, with no self-activation:

q˙i=α∏j≠i11+qj n−qi,i=1,…,N.\dot q_i=\alpha\prod_{j\ne i}\frac{1}{1+q_j^{\,n}}-q_i,\qquad i=1,\dots,N.(44)

The totals are in units of the repression constant and time in removal lifetimes. All arrows are composite, and the model is symmetric and all-to-all.

Lemma: a stable state has at most one raised node. At a fixed point qi=α(1+qin)/Πq_i=\alpha(1+q_i^n)/\Pi with Π=∏j(1+qjn)\Pi=\prod_j(1+q_j^n), so qi/(1+qin)=α/Πq_i/(1+q_i^n)=\alpha/\Pi takes the same value at every node. The shape of x/(1+xn)x/(1+x^n) splits the proof into two cases, 0<n≤10<n\le1 and n>1n>1. Its derivative is (1+(1−n)xn)/(1+xn)2\big(1+(1-n)x^n\big)/(1+x^n)^2. For 0<n≤10<n\le1 it is positive everywhere, so all nodes share one value, and the uniform state, the root of q=α/(1+qn)N−1q=\alpha/(1+q^n)^{N-1}, is the only fixed point. No node is raised. For n>1n>1 the function rises to a peak at xm=(n−1)−1/nx_m=(n-1)^{-1/n} and then falls, so each node sits on the rising or the falling side at that common level. Suppose two nodes a and b sit on the falling side. They then share one value q. The Jacobian of eq. (44) has off-diagonal entries −qi nqjn−1/(1+qjn)-q_i\,nq_j^{n-1}/(1+q_j^n), and applied to ea−ebe_a-e_b it returns (nqn/(1+qn)−1)(ea−eb)\big(nq^n/(1+q^n)-1\big)(e_a-e_b). On the falling side q>xmq>x_m, so nqn/(1+qn)>1nq^n/(1+q^n)>1 and the eigenvalue is positive. The state is unstable. So a stable state raises at most one node.

The count of N + 1 is a grid result, not a theorem. The lemma allows the N single winners and the uniform state. A numerical enumeration of every fixed point over α\alpha from 1.2 to 1000 and n from 1 to 8 finds at most 2 stable states at N=2N=2 and at most N+1N+1 for N from 3 to 12, the N single winners plus the uniform state. They coexist at small α\alpha and steep repression. Brute-force runs from many starts agree for N from 2 to 5, and at n=1n=1 every case has one stable state (numerical), as the first case of the lemma requires. A bound for all parameters was not proved.

Self-activation would change the architecture and the count. A Hill network of N self-activating switches with weak cross-repression reaches 2N2^N states. So the comparison with MultiFate in §18 and §19 is a comparison of two architectures within one framework, not a limit of one mechanism. The strict limit comparison for multistability is §16.

Bound the repertoire of symmetric Hill mutual repression by the one-raised-node lemma, and quote its N+1N+1 count with its model and grid: symmetric, all-to-all, product form, no self-activation.

18MultiFate's dimer pool solves in closed form

In MultiFate every factor dimerizes through one shared domain. Homodimers activate and heterodimers do not. One equilibrium then supplies both the steepness of self-activation and the inhibition by sharing partners.

1 · Model. Each factor XiX_i pairs with itself into an active homodimer and with any other factor into an inactive heterodimer.12 All factors share one dimerization domain, so every unordered pair of monomers associates at the same rate per pair. Count pairs in a volume V first. With nin_i molecules of XiX_i there are ni(ni−1)/2≈ni2/2n_i(n_i-1)/2\approx n_i^2/2 same-factor pairs and ninjn_in_j mixed pairs with XjX_j. Dividing by V2V^2 converts these to Xi2/2X_i^2/2 and XiXjX_iX_j in concentration units. So, per product of concentrations, the heterodimer channel runs twice as fast as the homodimer channel. We take the rate law of one homodimer association event to be k+Xi2k_+X_i^2, each event using two monomers, which puts the factor 2 on the heterodimer arrow. With one dissociation constant for every dimer,

Xi+Xi⇌k−k+CXiXi,Xi+Xj⇌k−2k+CXiXj  (j≠i),Kd=k−k+.X_i+X_i\xrightleftharpoons[k_-]{k_+}C_{X_iX_i},\qquad X_i+X_j\xrightleftharpoons[k_-]{2k_+}C_{X_iX_j}\ \ (j\ne i),\qquad K_d=\frac{k_-}{k_+}.(45)

Homodimer association has rate law k+Xi2k_+X_i^2, heterodimer association 2k+XiXj2k_+X_iX_j, and every dimer dissociates at k−k_-. Equilibrium therefore gives CXiXi=Xi2/KdC_{X_iX_i}=X_i^2/K_d and CXiXj=2XiXj/KdC_{X_iX_j}=2X_iX_j/K_d, the statistical convention of Zhu and colleagues (supplement, p. 8). The totals count each homodimer twice:

qXi=Xi+2CXiXi+∑j≠iCXiXj.q_{X_i}=X_i+2C_{X_iX_i}+\sum_{j\ne i}C_{X_iX_j}.(46)

The homodimer activates its own gene through composite transcription and translation, and every state is removed at one frequency δ\delta, "regardless of its dimerization state" (Box 1, p. 6 of 11):

q˙Xi=α+β CXiXi nKM n+CXiXi n−δ qXi.\dot q_{X_i}=\alpha+\beta\,\frac{C_{X_iX_i}^{\,n}}{K_M^{\,n}+C_{X_iX_i}^{\,n}}-\delta\,q_{X_i}.(47)

Here α\alpha is basal production, β\beta activated production, KMK_M the homodimer level for half activation and n the transcriptional Hill coefficient. These are MultiFate's letters, and β\beta is not Gardner's coefficient of §15. The published dimensionless values are α=0.8\alpha=0.8, β=20\beta=20, Kd=1K_d=1 and n=1.5n=1.5, in units of KMK_M and 1/δ1/\delta (reported). Dimerization is fast: the authors estimate unbinding at 14.4 per hour against removal at 0.1 per hour (supplement, parameter section).

Every monomer keeps the same free fraction, which closes the binding layer. Substituting the equilibria into eq. (46), qXi=Xi(1+2F/Kd)q_{X_i}=X_i\big(1+2F/K_d\big) with F=∑jXjF=\sum_jX_j the free monomer of all factors. The factor in parentheses is the same for every i, so Xi=φ qXiX_i=\varphi\,q_{X_i} with one shared φ=1/(1+2F/Kd)\varphi=1/(1+2F/K_d). Summing over i, the pooled total S=∑iqXiS=\sum_iq_{X_i} satisfies F=φSF=\varphi S, so 2(S/Kd)φ2+φ−1=02(S/K_d)\varphi^2+\varphi-1=0, and

φ=21+1+8S/Kd,CXiXi=φ2qXi2Kd.\varphi=\frac{2}{1+\sqrt{1+8S/K_d}},\qquad C_{X_iX_i}=\frac{\varphi^2q_{X_i}^2}{K_d}.(48)

Every other factor inhibits XiX_i through φ\varphi, by taking a share of the partners.

The homodimer is nearly quadratic in its own total while it is dilute or holds a small share of the pool. With the other totals held, ∂S/∂qXi=1\partial S/\partial q_{X_i}=1, so the own-total log-slope of the homodimer is

∂ln⁡CXiXi∂ln⁡qXi=2+2qXiφ′(S)φ(S)=2−8qXi/Kdw(1+w),w=1+8S/Kd.\frac{\partial\ln C_{X_iX_i}}{\partial\ln q_{X_i}}=2+\frac{2q_{X_i}\varphi'(S)}{\varphi(S)}=2-\frac{8q_{X_i}/K_d}{w(1+w)},\qquad w=\sqrt{1+8S/K_d}.(49)

It is close to 2 while 8qXi/Kd≪w(1+w)8q_{X_i}/K_d\ll w(1+w). Two cases satisfy that condition: a dilute factor, qXi≪Kdq_{X_i}\ll K_d, whatever its share, and a factor holding a small share of a large pool, qXi≪Sq_{X_i}\ll S. The slope falls toward 1 only when one factor dominates a large pool. For a factor alone it is 1.96, 1.75, 1.33, 1.11 and 1.04 at qXi/Kd=0.01q_{X_i}/K_d=0.01, 0.1, 1, 10 and 100. With 20Kd20K_d held by others, one factor ON, it stays at 2.00, 2.00 and 1.96 up to qXi=Kdq_{X_i}=K_d and falls to 1.69 and 1.19 at 10 and 100 (exact, Figure 7). An OFF factor rising among ON factors is therefore nearly quadratic, a Hill degree of 2 made by binding.

Solve a shared dimerization pool through the common free fraction (48), write the statistical factor of 2 into the heterodimer arrow, and read the binding-made cooperativity from eq. (49), close to 2 while 8qXi/Kd≪w(1+w)8q_{X_i}/K_d\ll w(1+w), that is while the factor is dilute or holds a small share of a large pool.

19Counting MultiFate's stable states, and what removal decides

The stable states of MultiFate are counted by numerical enumeration of the closed loop. The count follows binomial sums whose range is set by how many factors can stay ON together. The removal rule decides whether partner competition sets the count at all.

5 · Close the loop. At a fixed point each node solves one scalar equation at the shared φ\varphi, δqXi=α+βh(φ2qXi2/Kd)\delta q_{X_i}=\alpha+\beta h\big(\varphi^2q_{X_i}^2/K_d\big), where h is the activation law of eq. (47). That equation has a low, a middle and a high branch. A fixed point is therefore a pattern of nodes over the three branches, plus one scalar consistency equation for S. Enumerating every pattern and solving its equation finds every fixed point the branch parametrization can reach, and the eigenvalues of the Jacobian classify each one. This is a numerical enumeration, not a certified one. Brute-force runs from 300 to 500 starts agree for N from 2 to 5 (numerical).

The counts follow binomial sums. At the published parameters the stable states number

N23456789101112
stable states371530569993130176232299
most factors ON23444433333

(numerical). Every count is a sum over the allowed numbers k of factors ON together,

stable states=∑k=kminkmax(Nk),\text{stable states}=\sum_{k=k_\mathrm{min}}^{k_\mathrm{max}}\binom{N}{k},(50)

where kmaxk_\mathrm{max} is the most factors ON and kmink_\mathrm{min} is 1, or 0 once the all-OFF state is stable, which happens from N = 7. For N = 4 every non-empty subset is allowed, 24−1=152^4-1=15. For N = 5, one to four ON gives 5+10+10+5=305+10+10+5=30. For N = 9, zero to three ON gives 1+9+36+84=1301+9+36+84=130.

Sharing partners caps how many factors stay ON. With k factors ON, each near its full level β/δ=20\beta/\delta=20, the pool is S≈20kS\approx20k. For a large pool eq. (48) gives φ2≈Kd/(2S)\varphi^2\approx K_d/(2S), so each ON homodimer is about q2/(2S)≈10/kq^2/(2S)\approx10/k and falls as 1/k. At the published parameters that holds at most four factors ON for N≤7N\le7 and three for N≥8N\ge8. Zhu and colleagues give the same reason, the diminishing share of active homodimers among all dimers (p. 9 of 11).

Measurement and a reanalysis

Zhu and colleagues built MultiFate-3 in mammalian cells, and the cells held seven distinct states, each stable for at least 18 days (p. 1 of 11). Seven is the count at N = 3. For larger N they report a maximum of 256 attractors at N = 9 in the same model (p. 9 of 11).12 Our reanalysis finds 130 stable states there, and 256=130+(94)=130+126256=130+\binom94=130+126. The 126 are the symmetric four-ON fixed points, which exist on the middle branch with a threefold unstable eigenvalue of +0.0546 δ+0.0546\,\delta (and +0.0245 δ+0.0245\,\delta at N = 8). A kick of 0.1% sends each to a three-ON state (numerical). Their counts of robust attractors, read from their Fig. 5D as about 92 and 128 at N = 8 and 9, agree with our stable counts of 93 and 130.

Binding supplies the steepness. Without transcriptional cooperativity, n=1n=1, a parameter set chosen for three states at N = 2 (α=0.4\alpha=0.4, β=20\beta=20, Kd=0.1K_d=0.1) holds 3, 7, 15, 31, 62, 119 and 218 states for N = 2 to 8, following 2N−12^N-1 up to N = 5 (numerical). The near-quadratic homodimer of eq. (49) does the work. Zhu and colleagues also report multistability at n=1n=1 (supplement, p. 19).

Heterodimers make the OFF states. A lone factor always activates itself at the published parameters. It stays OFF only because ON factors, or the pooled basal expression of many OFF factors, titrate its monomers into inactive heterodimers. Forbidding heterodimers leaves one stable state, all ON, for every N (numerical).

Under free-only removal the steady-state equations separate, but the dynamics stay coupled. Remove only free monomers: q˙Xi=α+βh(Xi2/Kd)−δXi=gi(Xi)\dot q_{X_i}=\alpha+\beta h(X_i^2/K_d)-\delta X_i=g_i(X_i). Each right side depends on its own free monomer alone, so at a fixed point each XiX_i is a root of one scalar sigmoidal equation, with one or three roots. The dynamics do not separate. In logarithmic free coordinates y=ln⁡Xy=\ln X, eq. (46) gives q˙=Ay˙\dot q=A\dot y with the binding-capacity matrix Aij=∂qXi/∂ln⁡XjA_{ij}=\partial q_{X_i}/\partial\ln X_j, whose off-diagonal entries 2XiXj/Kd2X_iX_j/K_d are not zero. So y˙=A−1g(ey)\dot y=A^{-1}g(e^{y}), and the Jacobian at a fixed point is A−1GA^{-1}G with G=diag(gi′Xi)G=\mathrm{diag}(g_i'X_i). Since A is symmetric positive definite, A−1GA^{-1}G is similar to A−1/2GA−1/2A^{-1/2}GA^{-1/2}, which has the inertia of G by Sylvester's law. The unstable directions are the nodes on a middle root. So the count is exactly 2N2^N when the scalar equation has three roots and 1 otherwise, for every N. At the published parameters it is 1, all ON.
