At Kd=30K_d=30 it is 2N2^N, while uniform removal gives 4, 7, 11, 16, 22 and 29 for N = 2 to 7 (numerical). Uniform removal, the published model, is what lets partner competition set the count.

Count stable states from the closed loop by enumerating branch patterns, expect binomial sums (50) with a co-expression cap set by partner sharing, and name the removal rule, since free-only removal turns the count into 1 or 2N2^N through Sylvester's law.

Part 5

Adaptation

One incoherent feedforward loop, built two ways. Both effective laws compute input over controller. In binding and catalysis each needs its own regime of its binding pair, and the input itself walks the controller across the map. The core shows the step, the pulse and the controller.

20One feedforward loop, two implementations, two production constants

The controller can degrade the output or repress its gene. Matching the two set points fixes two different production constants, one per design, and the matching condition carries units.

Adaptation is a return to the old output after a sustained change of input. In an incoherent feedforward loop the input u drives the output X directly and also drives a controller Y that opposes X. The test here is a tenfold step: hold u=u0u=u_0 until steady state, step to 10u010u_0, and compute the steady-state error

ε(u0)=qX∗(10u0)qX∗(u0)−1.\varepsilon(u_0)=\frac{q_X^*(10u_0)}{q_X^*(u_0)}-1 .(51)

A persistent adaptive window is a range of u0u_0, open toward one end of the input range, on which ∣ε∣≤0.1|\varepsilon|\le0.1. An isolated input at which ε\varepsilon changes sign is a protocol-dependent endpoint cancellation, not a window, because it moves when the step factor changes.

1 · Model. The input is dimensionless and multiplies both production laws, as an activator held in its linear range or a gene dosage would. In both designs the controller is made by ∅⇝Y\varnothing\rightsquigarrow Y with rate law k2uk_2u and leaves every state that contains it at frequency γ\gamma. In the degradation design Y binds X and destroys it. Binding is an elementary pair, and at this model's resolution the catalytic step is one event:

∅⇝X  (rate law k1,Du),X+Y⇌k−k+CXY,CXY→kcatY,Y⇝∅,  CXY⇝X  (total rate law γqY),q˙X=k1,Du−kcatCXY,q˙Y=k2u−γqY.\begin{aligned}&\varnothing\rightsquigarrow X\ \ (\text{rate law }k_{1,\mathrm D}u),\qquad X+Y\xrightleftharpoons[k_-]{k_+}C_{XY},\qquad C_{XY}\xrightarrow{k_\mathrm{cat}}Y,\\ &Y\rightsquigarrow\varnothing,\ \ C_{XY}\rightsquigarrow X\ \ (\text{total rate law }\gamma q_Y),\qquad \dot q_X=k_{1,\mathrm D}u-k_\mathrm{cat}C_{XY},\quad \dot q_Y=k_2u-\gamma q_Y .\end{aligned}(52)

The composite step CXY⇝XC_{XY}\rightsquigarrow X returns the bound output to the free pool when its controller is removed, so X leaves the system only through catalysis. This is an idealized controller-removal model, not indiscriminate dilution of every molecule, and the exact adaptation of free X below depends on it. The totals are qX=X+CXYq_X=X+C_{XY} and qY=Y+CXYq_Y=Y+C_{XY}, and binding is at equilibrium, KdCXY=XYK_dC_{XY}=XY.

In the repression design the controller binds the promoter instead. Y binds the promoter G of the gene for X, whose total qGq_G is fixed. Only the free promoter expresses, and X binds nothing:

G+Y⇌k−k+CGY,G⇝G+X  (rate law k1,Ru G/qG),X⇝∅  (rate law δqX),Y⇝∅,  CGY⇝G  (total rate law γqY),q˙X=k1,Ru GqG−δqX,q˙Y=k2u−γqY.\begin{aligned}&G+Y\xrightleftharpoons[k_-]{k_+}C_{GY},\qquad G\rightsquigarrow G+X\ \ (\text{rate law }k_{1,\mathrm R}u\,G/q_G),\qquad X\rightsquigarrow\varnothing\ \ (\text{rate law }\delta q_X),\\ &Y\rightsquigarrow\varnothing,\ \ C_{GY}\rightsquigarrow G\ \ (\text{total rate law }\gamma q_Y),\qquad \dot q_X=k_{1,\mathrm R}u\,\frac{G}{q_G}-\delta q_X,\quad \dot q_Y=k_2u-\gamma q_Y .\end{aligned}(53)

The totals are qG=G+CGYq_G=G+C_{GY} and qY=Y+CGYq_Y=Y+C_{GY}, with KdCGY=GYK_dC_{GY}=GY, and qX=Xq_X=X. The two production constants carry different subscripts because the designs will need different values. The observable is the output total qXq_X, and in the degradation design free X is a second readout. A check against the full mass-action networks confirms binding equilibrium on the clock of the totals, to within 6.6×10−56.6\times10^{-5} over a step (numerical).

2 · Limit. Each design has a standard effective law. Degradation becomes a Michaelis-Menten law in which the substrate total stands for the free substrate, eq. (5). Repression becomes a Hill law of coefficient 1 in which the repressor total stands for the free repressor, the trace-promoter cut of eq. (6):

q˙X=k1,Du−kcat qY qXKd+qX  (degradation),q˙X=k1,Ru KdKd+qY−δqX  (repression).\dot q_X=k_{1,\mathrm D}u-k_\mathrm{cat}\,q_Y\,\frac{q_X}{K_d+q_X}\ \ \text{(degradation)},\qquad \dot q_X=k_{1,\mathrm R}u\,\frac{K_d}{K_d+q_Y}-\delta q_X\ \ \text{(repression)}.(54)

3 · Match. In both designs the controller settles at qY∗=k2u/γq_Y^*=k_2u/\gamma, proportional to the input. The degradation law then gives k1,Du=kcatqY∗X∗/(Kd+X∗)k_{1,\mathrm D}u=k_\mathrm{cat}q_Y^*X^*/(K_d+X^*), so

X∗=Kd ρ1−ρ,ρ=k1,D γkcat k2,X^*=K_d\,\frac{\rho}{1-\rho},\qquad \rho=\frac{k_{1,\mathrm D}\,\gamma}{k_\mathrm{cat}\,k_2},(55)

independent of the input whenever the dimensionless degrader load ρ\rho is below 1. The repression law gives X∗→k1,RKdγ/(δk2)X^*\to k_{1,\mathrm R}K_d\gamma/(\delta k_2) once qY≫Kdq_Y\gg K_d, also independent of the input. Equal set points therefore require

k1,R=δγ k2 ρ1−ρ.k_{1,\mathrm R}=\frac{\delta}{\gamma}\,k_2\,\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}.(56)

Both sides are a production rate per unit input, a concentration per time, because δ/γ\delta/\gamma and ρ\rho are dimensionless. Take KdK_d as the unit of concentration and 1/γ1/\gamma as the unit of time, and set k2=γKdk_2=\gamma K_d per unit input, so that qY∗=uKdq_Y^*=uK_d. The illustrative values kcat=1000γk_\mathrm{cat}=1000\gamma, ρ=0.05\rho=0.05 and δ=10γ\delta=10\gamma then give k1,D=ρkcatk2/γ=50 γKdk_{1,\mathrm D}=\rho k_\mathrm{cat}k_2/\gamma=50\,\gamma K_d and k1,R=(10/19) γKd≈0.526 γKdk_{1,\mathrm R}=(10/19)\,\gamma K_d\approx0.526\,\gamma K_d per unit input, and a shared set point X∗=Kd/19=0.0526 KdX^*=K_d/19=0.0526\,K_d (exact). In their limits both laws compute the ratio of input to controller. That shared structure is why the effective laws call the two designs the same.

Match two implementations by their set points, not by one shared constant: write each production constant with its own symbol and derive the matching condition, here eq. (56), with its units.

21The degradation design adapts only while both partners are free

The degradation design cancels the input exactly in free X at every input. Its total output adapts only while the degrader stays free and well below its dissociation constant, and the input pushes it out of that regime.

4 · Move a total. Here the input itself moves a total, because qY∗=uKdq_Y^*=uK_d. A sweep of the input walks the controller total along the pair's map.

The binding-catalysis steady state is exact in closed form. Setting eq. (52) to zero gives CXY∗=k1,Du/kcatC^*_{XY}=k_{1,\mathrm D}u/k_\mathrm{cat} and qY∗=k2u/γq_Y^*=k_2u/\gamma, so CXY∗/qY∗=ρC^*_{XY}/q_Y^*=\rho and Y∗=(1−ρ)qY∗Y^*=(1-\rho)q_Y^*. Binding then gives the free output and the total:

X∗=Kd CXY∗Y∗=Kd ρ1−ρ,qX∗=X∗+CXY∗=X∗ (1+η),η=Y∗Kd=CXY∗X∗.X^*=K_d\,\frac{C^*_{XY}}{Y^*}=K_d\,\frac{\rho}{1-\rho},\qquad q_X^*=X^*+C^*_{XY}=X^*\,(1+\eta),\qquad \eta=\frac{Y^*}{K_d}=\frac{C^*_{XY}}{X^*}.(57)

The free output is the effective law's set point (55) at every input. The total carries an extra factor, 1+η1+\eta. Here η\eta is Lecture 8's residual fraction of the output total: the bound share measured against the winner, free X.

Precision demands depth inside the adaptive regime. A tenfold step multiplies Y∗Y^*, and so η\eta, by ten. By eq. (57) the error of the total is

ε=1+10η1+η−1=9η1+η,∣ε∣≤0.1  ⟺  η≤0.18.9=0.0112.\varepsilon=\frac{1+10\eta}{1+\eta}-1=\frac{9\eta}{1+\eta},\qquad |\varepsilon|\le0.1\iff\eta\le\frac{0.1}{8.9}=0.0112 .(58)

With Y∗=(1−ρ)qYY^*=(1-\rho)q_Y, the persistent window is qY≤0.0112Kd/(1−ρ)=0.0118 Kdq_Y\le0.0112K_d/(1-\rho)=0.0118\,K_d (exact). Its edge sits at 0.0112 times the regime boundary Y∗=KdY^*=K_d, two decades inside the regime. That is Lecture 8's bounded-factor accuracy read backwards: a 10% tolerance asks for the discarded term to be about 1% of the winner. Free X has ε=0\varepsilon=0 at every input.

The Michaelis-Menten law is valid exactly where the design works. The law (54) needs the free substrate to win its own total, X≈qXX\approx q_X, which is the regime (Y,X)(Y,X) or (CXY,X)(C_{XY},X) of the table.1 So the law describes the adaptive regime correctly, and it has no complex with which to represent the failure: sequestration of the total output.

Loading the degrader more heavily widens the window and makes the set point fragile. From eq. (55), ln⁡X∗=ln⁡Kd+ln⁡ρ−ln⁡(1−ρ)\ln X^*=\ln K_d+\ln\rho-\ln(1-\rho), so dln⁡X∗/dln⁡ρ=1/(1−ρ)d\ln X^*/d\ln\rho=1/(1-\rho): 1.05 at ρ=0.05\rho=0.05, 2 at 0.5 and 10 at 0.9. In the plane of input and set point, eq. (58) puts the window edge at u0=0.0112 (1+X∗/Kd)u_0=0.0112\,(1+X^*/K_d), which rises with the load (Figure 9, left). For ρ≥1\rho\ge1 production outruns the degrader's capacity kcatqYk_\mathrm{cat}q_Y, and X accumulates without bound. Saturating the degrader therefore trades robustness of the set point for range.

Diluting the output as well closes the window from below, and gives Du and colleagues' form. Let every X-containing state also be removed at dXd_X, so a bound X is diluted and releases its degrader. The steady state then balances k1,Du=kcatCXY∗+dXqX∗k_{1,\mathrm D}u=k_\mathrm{cat}C^*_{XY}+d_Xq_X^*, with CXY∗=X∗Y∗/KdC^*_{XY}=X^*Y^*/K_d and qX∗=X∗(1+Y∗/Kd)q_X^*=X^*(1+Y^*/K_d). Solving,

qX∗=k1,DudX⋅Kd+Y∗Kd+(1+kcat/dX) Y∗.q_X^*=\frac{k_{1,\mathrm D}u}{d_X}\cdot\frac{K_d+Y^*}{K_d+(1+k_\mathrm{cat}/d_X)\,Y^*}.(59)

The first factor is the unregulated level. In Du and colleagues' scaled variables, with dosage D, free regulator rs≈Dr_s\approx D and the dimensionless catalytic rate k~c=kcat/dX\tilde k_c=k_\mathrm{cat}/d_X, this is their mtot=D(K+rs)/(K+(k~c+1)rs)m_\mathrm{tot}=D(K+r_s)/(K+(\tilde k_c+1)r_s) (Data S1, pp. 14 to 16).13 It compensates dosage only approximately, and only for K/(k~c+1)<D≪KK/(\tilde k_c+1)<D\ll K. Their K also counts removal of the complex, so it is a Briggs-Haldane-like constant that reduces to KdK_d when binding is fast. With dX=γd_X=\gamma and kcat=1000γk_\mathrm{cat}=1000\gamma the best error of a tenfold step is 19.1%, and no input adapts within 10%. A 10% window needs kcat/dXk_\mathrm{cat}/d_X above about 3500 (numerical). The repression design has no such lower edge, because its output is removed at first order anyway.

Model prediction and measurement

Bleris and colleagues built incoherent feedforward loops in mammalian cells, with a microRNA as the controller. Their measured loops adapted to the amount of their genetic template (abstract; p. 7). Their model predicted a loss of adaptation at high copy number and low silencing-complex concentration, from saturation of that complex (p. 5).14 In the language of the table this is the degrader-saturated regime (CXY,X)(C_{XY},X). It is their model's prediction, not a measurement.

Check a degradation design by the residual fraction η=Y∗/Kd\eta=Y^*/K_d of its output total: a tenfold step adapts within 10% only while η≤0.0112\eta\le0.0112, free output adapts regardless, and output dilution adds a lower edge that needs kcat/dXk_\mathrm{cat}/d_X in the thousands.

22The repression design adapts only above its dissociation constant and its promoter

The repression design adapts only while the repressor exceeds both its dissociation constant and the promoter total. The Hill law sees the first condition. Only the binding-catalysis model sees the second, and with it a titration switch and a cancellation that holds for one step size.

The binding-catalysis steady state reads the free promoter. Eq. (53) at steady state gives qX∗=k1,Ru G/(δqG)q_X^*=k_{1,\mathrm R}u\,G/(\delta q_G), with G the free member of the pair (G,Y)(G,Y) at totals (qG,uKd)(q_G,uK_d). By the same quadratic as eq. (4),

G=12[(qG−qY−Kd)+(qG−qY−Kd)2+4KdqG],ε=10 G(10u0)G(u0)−1.G=\tfrac12\Big[(q_G-q_Y-K_d)+\sqrt{(q_G-q_Y-K_d)^2+4K_dq_G}\Big],\qquad \varepsilon=\frac{10\,G(10u_0)}{G(u_0)}-1 .(60)

The regimes of the pair G, Y place both failures. Name each regime by the winner of qGq_G, the promoter, then of qYq_Y:

RegimeLeading sectorFree promoter GGain of qX∗q_X^* in u
(G,Y)(G,Y), weak repressionqY≪Kdq_Y\ll K_d, qG≪Kdq_G\ll K_d≈qG\approx q_G1, tracks the input
(G,CGY)(G,C_{GY}), repressor titratedqY≪qGq_Y\ll q_G, qG≫Kdq_G\gg K_d≈qG\approx q_G1, tracks
(CGY,CGY)(C_{GY},C_{GY})qG≫Kdq_G\gg K_d, ∣qY−qG∣≪KdqG|q_Y-q_G|\ll\sqrt{K_dq_G}≈KdqG\approx\sqrt{K_dq_G}a switch
(CGY,Y)(C_{GY},Y), repressor in excessqY≫qGq_Y\gg q_G, qY≫Kdq_Y\gg K_d≈KdqG/qY\approx K_dq_G/q_Y0, adapts

Each entry is leading order deep inside its sector. Near the ray of a heavy promoter, outside the rounding scale KdqG\sqrt{K_dq_G}, the improved expressions are G≈qG−qYG\approx q_G-q_Y below it and G≈KdqG/(qY−qG)G\approx K_dq_G/(q_Y-q_G) above it, and the exact root (60) covers the rest. The exact ties lie within a factor of 2 of the sector lines, as in §2.

The design needs (CGY,Y)(C_{GY},Y): the free repressor wins its own total and the complex wins the promoter's. There the free-promoter readout has gain −1-1 in the repressor total, and the input's gain of +1+1 cancels it.

The Hill law already predicts the low-input failure, weak repression. In the Hill law (54) the output is proportional to u/(1+u)u/(1+u) in units of KdK_d, so

ε=10(1+u0)1+10u0−1=91+10u0=9KdKd+10qY,∣ε∣≤0.1  ⟺  qY≥8.9 Kd.\varepsilon=\frac{10(1+u_0)}{1+10u_0}-1=\frac{9}{1+10u_0}=\frac{9K_d}{K_d+10q_Y},\qquad |\varepsilon|\le0.1\iff q_Y\ge8.9\,K_d .(61)

At u0=0.01u_0=0.01 it gives 818%. At low input the repressor is scarce, the promoter stays mostly free, and production tracks the input. This is weak repression, and the Hill law represents it.

The Hill law misses titration of the repressor by the promoter pool. With a light promoter, qG=0.1Kdq_G=0.1K_d, eq. (60) starts the persistent window at 8.12Kd8.12K_d, close to the Hill law. With a heavy promoter, qG=10Kdq_G=10K_d, the first qGq_G of repressor is soaked up by the sites, and the persistent window starts only at 80.5Kd80.5K_d (numerical). In both cases the window begins about one decade beyond the leading-order regime boundary qY=max⁡(Kd,qG)q_Y=\max(K_d,q_G).

Below that window the heavy promoter has a protocol-dependent endpoint cancellation. At qG=10Kdq_G=10K_d the error of eq. (60) passes through zero at qY=2.0404 Kdq_Y=2.0404\,K_d, and stays within ±0.1\pm0.1 from 1.9039Kd1.9039K_d to 2.2107Kd2.2107K_d (exact roots, Figure 10). A tenfold step from there jumps across the titration ray qY=qGq_Y=q_G: the input rises tenfold while the free promoter falls about tenfold as the repressor passes the pool. The two endpoints happen to give the same output. Between them the output does not stay flat, and a different step factor moves the cancelling input. It is not an adaptive window.

On the titration ray a step over-adapts. At qG=10Kdq_G=10K_d the high-input step u=10→100u=10\to100 starts on the ray, where the free promoter is about KdqG\sqrt{K_dq_G}. The step drives the promoter into (CGY,Y)(C_{GY},Y), and the output settles at 0.41 of its old level, an error of −59%-59\% (numerical). The Hill law, with its promoter in trace, has no ray to cross.

Measurement

Segall-Shapiro, Sontag and Voigt tuned a monomeric TALE repressor to stay in excess at the lowest gene dosage, and obtained nearly constant expression across plasmids from 3 to 100 copies per cell, at the price of output strength (pp. 353 to 354).15 Their model assumes exactly the two conditions above, a repressor in excess of the promoters and of its KdK_d (supplement Note 1, pp. 3 to 5), and gives the strength-error trade as S=E/(E+1)S=E/(E+1) (supplement Eq. 19). Goentoro and colleagues likewise ask for Y/K>10Y/K>10 and note that the promoter then runs at a small fraction of its maximal strength (p. 897).16 At the edge of the light-promoter window here the promoter runs at 1/(1+8.12)=11%1/(1+8.12)=11\% of its unrepressed strength.

Check a repression design against both of its conditions, qY≫Kdq_Y\gg K_d and qY≫qGq_Y\gg q_G, at the lowest input it must handle, and distinguish a persistent window from an endpoint cancellation by asking whether it survives a different step factor.

23Step responses: what each effective law misses

The closed dynamics show both failures in one experiment. Each effective law misses a different one, for a different reason.

5 · Close the loop. Step the input tenfold from the steady state and integrate the closed totals, with binding solved at every instant (Figure 11). At low input, u=0.01→0.1u=0.01\to0.1, the degradation design starts in (Y,X)(Y,X). Its total pulses 5.9-fold and returns to within 8.5%. The repression design starts in (G,Y)(G,Y) and rises about tenfold and stays there, with errors of 824% at qG=0.1Kdq_G=0.1K_d and 892% at 10Kd10K_d. At high input, u=10→100u=10\to100, the roles swap. The light-promoter repression design starts in (CGY,Y)(C_{GY},Y), pulses 4.9-fold and returns to within 8.1%. The degradation design starts in (Y,CXY)(Y,C_{XY}). Its total settles at an error of 814%, while its free X pulses 17-fold and returns exactly (all numerical).

Each effective law misses a different failure. The Michaelis-Menten law misses sequestration of the total output. It adapts at every input, with ε=0\varepsilon=0, and at high input it pulses to 18.4 and returns, while the binding-catalysis total stays 814% high. The Hill law captures the low-input failure, weak repression: its error of 818% at u0=0.01u_0=0.01 is close to the 824% of the light promoter. What it misses is depletion of free repressor by a finite promoter pool, and with it the titration that moves the window to 80.5Kd80.5K_d and the over-adaptation to 0.41 on the titration ray.

The readout matters as much as the regime. In the degradation design free X adapts exactly at every input, and only the total fails. Which pool counts is a biological question. The total counts when bound X still acts or is still measured, as for a fluorescent fusion, or for a target mRNA that is still translated while bound, until it is cleaved. The effective law cannot pose the question, because it has no complex.

Both loops forget the input only inside one regime. Each design adapts over a feasible operating range of inputs, set by its binding regime, never over every possible input. Lecture 10 asks what a loop must remember to adapt across a whole range, and it should take these claims with that scope.

Read a step response together with the regime before the step: the degradation design adapts from (Y,X)(Y,X) and the repression design from (CGY,Y)(C_{GY},Y), the Michaelis-Menten law misses sequestration of the total output, and the Hill law misses titration by the promoter pool.

Part 6

Oscillation

A ring of three repressors loses its symmetric rest state when each link amplifies more than twofold. A Hill law cannot supply that gain at coefficient 1. A finite promoter pool can, by titration, if bound repressor leaves with free repressor. Below the threshold a cycle can still coexist with a stable rest state. The core follows one cycle around the ring.

24A ring's rest state loses stability at a gain of 2 per link

Linearizing a symmetric ring gives a threshold on the gain of each link: 2 for proteins alone, a loop gain of 23=82^3=8, and 4/3 with an mRNA stage at equal lifetimes. Crossing it destabilizes the symmetric rest state. It is not a necessary condition for oscillation. A Hill law's gain is always below its coefficient.

The threshold comes from the eigenvalues of a cyclic matrix. Take a symmetric ring of three nodes with uniform removal, linearized at its symmetric steady state. Each node relaxes at rate 1, in units of its removal rate, and its upstream neighbour pushes it with slope −H-H. We call H>0H>0 the gain of each link. The loop gain, the product of the three link gains around the ring, is H3H^3. The Jacobian is J=−I−HPJ=-I-HP, with P the cyclic shift of the three nodes, whose eigenvalues are the cube roots of unity. So

μk=−1−H ωk,ω=e2πi/3,k=0,1,2.\mu_k=-1-H\,\omega^k,\qquad \omega=e^{2\pi i/3},\qquad k=0,1,2 .(62)

For k=1,2k=1,2, ωk=−12±i32\omega^k=-\tfrac12\pm i\tfrac{\sqrt3}2, so the pair has real part −1+H/2-1+H/2 and imaginary part ±H3/2\pm H\sqrt3/2. It crosses into the right half-plane at H=2H=2, a loop gain of 8, with frequency 3\sqrt3 times the removal rate. A ring of N genes, N odd, crosses at H=sec⁡(π/N)H=\sec(\pi/N). A two-gene loop instead becomes a saddle at H=1H=1, which was the toggle of §16.

The threshold is a statement about the symmetric rest state, not about oscillation in general. Above it the rest state is unstable. Below it the rest state is locally stable, yet a stable cycle can coexist with it far from rest, as §28 finds beyond a subcritical Hopf point. A gain above 2 per link is therefore sufficient to destabilize the rest state, and it is not necessary for a cycle.

An mRNA stage lowers the link threshold to 4/3 at best. Elowitz and Leibler's model adds an mRNA to each node (Box 1, p. 337):17

m˙i=−mi+α1+pi−1 n+α0,p˙i=−β (pi−mi).\dot m_i=-m_i+\frac{\alpha}{1+p_{i-1}^{\,n}}+\alpha_0,\qquad \dot p_i=-\beta\,(p_i-m_i).(63)

Here mim_i and pip_i are mRNA and protein in their authors' units, time is in mRNA lifetimes, α\alpha and α0\alpha_0 are the maximal and leaky transcription, and β\beta is the ratio of protein to mRNA removal rates. These letters hold only in this section. For a rotating mode the linearization gives (μ+1)(μ+β)=Hβe±iπ/3(\mu+1)(\mu+\beta)=H\beta e^{\pm i\pi/3}. Setting μ=iΩ\mu=i\Omega and separating real and imaginary parts gives Ω2=β(1−H/2)\Omega^2=\beta(1-H/2) and Ω(1+β)=Hβ3/2\Omega(1+\beta)=H\beta\sqrt3/2. Eliminating Ω\Omega, the rest state is unstable, for H<2H<2, exactly when

(1+β)2β<3H24−2H.\frac{(1+\beta)^2}{\beta}<\frac{3H^2}{4-2H}.(64)

This is Elowitz and Leibler's condition with their slope written as −H-H. The left side is smallest, 4, at β=1\beta=1, equal lifetimes, where the condition becomes H>4/3H>4/3. For H≥2H\ge2 the rest state is unstable at every β\beta.

A Hill law supplies a gain below its coefficient. The protein-only ring is p˙i=f(pi−1)−pi\dot p_i=f(p_{i-1})-p_i with f(x)=α0+α/(1+xn)f(x)=\alpha_0+\alpha/(1+x^n). At its unique symmetric fixed point, p∗=f(p∗)p^*=f(p^*),

H=∣f′(p∗)∣=n p∗n1+p∗n⋅p∗−α0p∗<n.H=|f'(p^*)|=\frac{n\,p^{*n}}{1+p^{*n}}\cdot\frac{p^*-\alpha_0}{p^*}<n .(65)

The first factor is below n and the second below 1, so a leak lowers the gain further. At n=1n=1, H<1H<1, below both thresholds, for every production, leak and pair of lifetimes. With Elowitz and Leibler's own parameters, n=2n=2, α=216.4\alpha=216.4, α0=0.2164\alpha_0=0.2164 and β=0.2\beta=0.2, derived from their Box 1, the gain is H=1.876H=1.876. The threshold of eq. (64) at β=0.2\beta=0.2 is 1.52, so the steady state is unstable, and the predicted period is 43.2 mRNA lifetimes, about 125 minutes (numerical). Their repressilator, built from cooperative repressors, oscillated with a period of around 150 minutes (p. 336, reported). The Hill law is the right model for that circuit.

Optional: why a Hill ring with coefficient 1 never oscillates, from any start

The local argument leaves open a cycle far from the steady state, and a global argument closes it. Let MiM_i and mim_i be the limsup and liminf of node i along a bounded trajectory. Each node passes its input through the decreasing map f(x)=α0+α/(1+x)f(x)=\alpha_0+\alpha/(1+x) and through stable first-order filters, so Mi≤f(mi−1)M_i\le f(m_{i-1}) and mi≥f(Mi−1)m_i\ge f(M_{i-1}). Around the ring this gives M≤F(m)M\le F(m) and m≥F(M)m\ge F(M) with F=f∘f∘fF=f\circ f\circ f, hence M≤F(F(M))M\le F(F(M)) and m≥F(F(m))m\ge F(F(m)).

Now f is a Möbius map, so F∘FF\circ F is again a Möbius map, and it has the same two fixed points as f: one positive and attracting, one negative. So F(F(x))<xF(F(x))<x above the positive steady state x∗x^* and F(F(x))>xF(F(x))>x below it. The two inequalities then force m=M=x∗m=M=x^*. Every trajectory converges, in the protein-only model and with mRNA, for every parameter and every odd ring length (exact).

The Hill limit in the literature

Potvin-Trottier and colleagues simulated a minimal Hill model of the repressilator at n=1n=1 (K=0.01K=0.01, λ=103\lambda=10^3). Its stochastic traces oscillate, while the deterministic equations with the same parameters show damped oscillations (Extended Data Fig. 4d and its legend; Supplementary Information 4.1, p. 12).18 The damping is the Hill limit of eq. (65).

Decide whether a repressor ring's symmetric rest state is stable by comparing the gain of each link with 2, a loop gain of 8, or with 4/3 when an mRNA stage has equal lifetimes. A gain above the threshold rules the rest state out, a gain below it does not rule out a cycle, and a Hill law supplies less than its coefficient.

25A finite promoter pool supplies the gain by titration

The same ring, written with its promoter sites, gets its gain from the titration layer of §16. The trace-promoter limit is the Hill ring with coefficient 1 and cannot oscillate.

1 · Model. Repressor Ri−1R_{i-1} binds the promoter sites PiP_i of gene i as a monomer, with indices counted around the ring of three. Free sites express at the full rate, every site, free or bound, leaks at a small rate, and free and bound repressor are diluted alike:

Ri−1+Pi⇌k−k+CPiRi−1,Pi⇝Pi+Ri  (rate law (kP+kℓ)Pi),CPiRi−1⇝CPiRi−1+Ri  (rate law kℓCPiRi−1),Ri⇝∅  (rate law λRi),CPi+1Ri⇝Pi+1  (rate law λCPi+1Ri).\begin{aligned}&R_{i-1}+P_i\xrightleftharpoons[k_-]{k_+}C_{P_iR_{i-1}},\\ &P_i\rightsquigarrow P_i+R_i\ \ (\text{rate law }(k_P+k_\ell)P_i),\qquad C_{P_iR_{i-1}}\rightsquigarrow C_{P_iR_{i-1}}+R_i\ \ (\text{rate law }k_\ell C_{P_iR_{i-1}}),\\ &R_i\rightsquigarrow\varnothing\ \ (\text{rate law }\lambda R_i),\qquad C_{P_{i+1}R_i}\rightsquigarrow P_{i+1}\ \ (\text{rate law }\lambda C_{P_{i+1}R_i}).\end{aligned}(66)

As in §16 the total balance is exact, and in units of qPq_P and 1/λ1/\lambda the closed loop is

r˙i=a(p(ri−1)+ε)−ri,i=1,2,3,\dot r_i=a\big(p(r_{i-1})+\varepsilon\big)-r_i,\qquad i=1,2,3,(67)

with ri=qRi/qPr_i=q_{R_i}/q_P, a=kP/λa=k_P/\lambda, ε=kℓ/kP\varepsilon=k_\ell/k_P and the free fraction p(r)p(r) of eq. (39). The observable is the three repressor totals over time.

2 · Limit. With the promoter in trace, p=κ/(κ+r)p=\kappa/(\kappa+r), and eq. (67) becomes the protein-only Hill ring with coefficient 1. By §24 it converges from every start. 3 · Match. In that limit the two rings are the same equations. At the reference parameters of §28 with the promoter put in trace, the gain is H=0.91H=0.91 and the run returns to rest (numerical).

4 · Move a total. With a finite pool, the gain is the titration slope. The gain of each link is the production slope relative to the removal slope of 1, H=a∣p′(r∗)∣=ap∗2/(p∗2+κ)H=a|p'(r^*)|=ap^{*2}/(p^{*2}+\kappa), with or without leak. At a leak-free steady state r∗=ap∗r^*=ap^*, and H equals the log-slope (40) of the free fraction at r∗r^*, which is eq. (42). So the ring can borrow the steep log-slope that titration makes near equivalence, up to about 12qP/K\tfrac12\sqrt{q_P/K} (Figure 6). In the irreversible limit κ→0\kappa\to0, below equivalence, r∗=a(1−r∗)r^*=a(1-r^*) and the gain is r∗/(1−r∗)=ar^*/(1-r^*)=a: the production per lifetime itself, without bound.

Write a repressor ring with its promoter sites, reduce it to eq. (67), and read the gain of each link as the titration slope ap∗2/(p∗2+κ)ap^{*2}/(p^{*2}+\kappa), which a finite pool can raise far above 2.

26The tightness threshold and its irreversible-binding edge

A leak-free monomer ring's symmetric steady state can lose stability only if the promoter pool exceeds 7+43≈13.97+4\sqrt3\approx13.9 dissociation constants. Production must then lie in a window. Irreversible binding is the edge of this map, where Clamons and Murray's idealized ring sits.

The threshold is a quadratic inequality in the free fraction. Set the gain (42) above 2 and clear the denominator: (1−p)(p+κ)>2(p2+κ)(1-p)(p+\kappa)>2(p^2+\kappa) becomes

3p∗2−(1−κ) p∗+κ<0.3p^{*2}-(1-\kappa)\,p^*+\kappa<0 .(68)

Some p∗p^* between 0 and 1 satisfies it exactly when the discriminant is positive, (1−κ)2>12κ(1-\kappa)^2>12\kappa, that is κ2−14κ+1>0\kappa^2-14\kappa+1>0. The root above 1 is excluded, so κ<7−43\kappa<7-4\sqrt3, or

qPK>17−43=7+43=(2+3)2≈13.93.\frac{q_P}{K}>\frac{1}{7-4\sqrt3}=7+4\sqrt3=(2+\sqrt3)^2\approx13.93 .(69)

This is exact for the leak-free symmetric ring under uniform removal.

Production must lie in a window. The roots of eq. (68) are p±=[(1−κ)±(1−κ)2−12κ]/6p_\pm=\big[(1-\kappa)\pm\sqrt{(1-\kappa)^2-12\kappa}\big]/6. Since a(p)=(1−p)(p+κ)/p2a(p)=(1-p)(p+\kappa)/p^2 falls as p rises, the steady state is unstable for

a(p+)<a<a(p−),which tends to2<a<2 qPKfor qPK≫1.a(p_+)<a<a(p_-),\qquad\text{which tends to}\qquad 2<a<2\,\frac{q_P}{K}\quad\text{for}\ \frac{q_P}{K}\gg1 .(70)

We call this the symmetric-state instability window, because that is what it bounds. It is not the complete set of parameters at which a cycle exists, as §28 shows.

The window's two edges have simple limits. They follow from p+→1/3p_+\to1/3 and p−→κp_-\to\kappa. At qP/K=200q_P/K=200 the window is 2.094<a<385.92.094<a<385.9, and the largest gain over production is 7.11, close to 12200\tfrac12\sqrt{200} (exact, leak-free). A leak raises the threshold slightly: to 14.1 at ε=10−3\varepsilon=10^{-3}, 16.1 at 10−210^{-2} and 20.8 at 3×10−23\times10^{-2} (numerical).

The threshold concerns the steady state, not every cycle. Eq. (69) is necessary and sufficient for the symmetric steady state to lose stability at some production. It does not prove that no cycle exists below it, because a subcritical Hopf point can leave a stable cycle beside a stable steady state, as §28 finds. A scan below the threshold found none: at qP/K=10q_P/K=10, 12, 13 and 13.5, with 26 productions from 1 to 316 and two distant starts each, every run came to rest (numerical).

Irreversible binding is the edge of the map, and Clamons and Murray's idealized ring sits there. As κ→0\kappa\to0, eq. (39) becomes p(r)=max⁡(0,1−r)p(r)=\max(0,1-r). Clamons and Murray's first-order CRISPRi model assumes abundant dCas, instantaneous binding and irreversible one-to-one binding of the guide-dCas complex to DNA, until the promoter pool saturates (p. 9).19 For the ring, with guide totals gig_i and promoter total P, their equation is

g˙i=αmax⁡(0,P−gi−1)+α0min⁡(P,gi−1)−γgi,\dot g_i=\alpha\max(0,P-g_{i-1})+\alpha_0\min(P,g_{i-1})-\gamma g_i ,(71)

where α\alpha and α0\alpha_0 are the guide production rates from an unbound and a bound promoter and γ\gamma is the dilution rate (p. 10). The loss γgi\gamma g_i multiplies the total guide, bound guide included, so this idealized equation dilutes bound complexes with free ones. In their full model, replication releases the DNA-bound complex back to the free pool rather than removing it (pp. 4 to 5), and the printed reaction list gives a different product for that step (p. 6). The comparison is therefore made on eq. (71).

A coefficient conversion maps eq. (71) onto the ring (67) at the edge. Since min⁡(P,g)=P−max⁡(0,P−g)\min(P,g)=P-\max(0,P-g),

αmax⁡(0,P−g)+α0min⁡(P,g)=α0P+(α−α0)max⁡(0,P−g).\alpha\max(0,P-g)+\alpha_0\min(P,g)=\alpha_0P+(\alpha-\alpha_0)\max(0,P-g).(72)

So their leak is a background from every promoter plus an increment from each free one, the lecture's form. With ri=gi/Pr_i=g_i/P and time in units of 1/γ1/\gamma,

r˙i=b+amax⁡(0,1−ri−1)−ri,a=α−α0γ,b=α0γ,\dot r_i=b+a\max(0,1-r_{i-1})-r_i,\qquad a=\frac{\alpha-\alpha_0}{\gamma},\qquad b=\frac{\alpha_0}{\gamma},(73)

which is eq. (67) at κ=0\kappa=0 with aε=ba\varepsilon=b, that is ε=α0/(α−α0)\varepsilon=\alpha_0/(\alpha-\alpha_0). At zero leak the two equations coincide exactly. Integrated side by side they give the same period, 3.808 in units of 1/γ1/\gamma, with a largest trajectory difference of 3.1×10−63.1\times10^{-6} (numerical).

Their instability condition needs the central state below saturation. If b<1b<1, the symmetric state lies on the sloped segment, r∗=(a+b)/(1+a)<1r^*=(a+b)/(1+a)<1, the gain is a, and the rotating pair has real part a/2−1a/2-1. It is unstable exactly when a>2a>2, that is (α−α0)/2>γ(\alpha-\alpha_0)/2>\gamma, the condition they derived (p. 11). If b>1b>1, the symmetric state is r∗=br^*=b, on the flat segment where production does not depend on the input, and the Jacobian is −I-I: stable. At b=1b=1 the state r∗=1r^*=1 sits on the kink, where the law has no derivative, so it is treated directly. A node below 1 never falls, since its rate is at least 1−ri>01-r_i>0, so every deficit shrinks at least as e−te^{-t}. A node above 1 adds nothing to the next node's production, so the deficit cannot travel around the ring, and every trajectory comes to rest at r∗=1r^*=1 (exact). So the complete condition is (α−α0)/2>γ(\alpha-\alpha_0)/2>\gamma together with α0<γ\alpha_0<\gamma. For example α=5\alpha=5, α0=2\alpha_0=2, γ=1\gamma=1 satisfies the first, with a=3a=3, but has b=2b=2, a saturated central state at r∗=2r^*=2, and a stable one (exact). Clamons and Murray state that cooperativity is not necessary for a toggle or a repressilator (p. 12). In the coordinates of this page their ring is the right edge of the map, qP/K→∞q_P/K\to\infty, where the window (70) becomes a>2a>2.

Test whether a monomer ring's symmetric state can lose stability against qP/K>7+43q_P/K>7+4\sqrt3 and the production window (70), read irreversible binding as the edge κ→0\kappa\to0 with the conversion (72), and require α0<γ\alpha_0<\gamma as well as (α−α0)/2>γ(\alpha-\alpha_0)/2>\gamma at that edge.

27The bound-to-free removal ratio rescales the pool

If bound repressor leaves at a fraction θ\theta of the rate of free repressor, the symmetric-state gain and the instability thresholds of the ring and the toggle are those of uniform removal with the pool qP/Kq_P/K replaced by θqP/K\theta q_P/K. Protected bound repressor, θ=0\theta=0, makes neither a toggle nor a cycle, from any start.

Partial protection changes the removal slope. Let free repressor leave at λf\lambda_\mathrm{f} and bound repressor at λb=θλf\lambda_\mathrm{b}=\theta\lambda_\mathrm{f}, with time in units of 1/λf1/\lambda_\mathrm{f}. The free repressor, in units of qPq_P, is ϱ(r)=r−1+p(r)\varrho(r)=r-1+p(r), so the ring becomes

r˙i=a(p(ri−1)+ε)−[θri+(1−θ)ϱ(ri)].\dot r_i=a\big(p(r_{i-1})+\varepsilon\big)-\big[\theta r_i+(1-\theta)\varrho(r_i)\big].(74)

The removal slope is θ+(1−θ)ϱ′\theta+(1-\theta)\varrho', and ϱ′=1+p′=κ/(p2+κ)\varrho'=1+p'=\kappa/(p^2+\kappa). Dividing the production slope by it, the gain is H=ap∗2/(θp∗2+κ)H=ap^{*2}/(\theta p^{*2}+\kappa).

At a leak-free steady state the gain is the uniform gain at a smaller pool. The steady state balances ap∗=θr∗+(1−θ)ϱ(r∗)ap^*=\theta r^*+(1-\theta)\varrho(r^*). With r(p)r(p) from eq. (39) and ϱ=(1−p)κ/p\varrho=(1-p)\kappa/p, this gives a=(1−p∗)(θp∗+κ)/p∗2a=(1-p^*)(\theta p^*+\kappa)/p^{*2}, and substituting,

H=(1−p∗)(θp∗+κ)θp∗2+κ,H(p;θ,κ)=H(p;1,κ/θ),a(p;θ,κ)=θ a(p;1,κ/θ).H=\frac{(1-p^*)(\theta p^*+\kappa)}{\theta p^{*2}+\kappa},\qquad H(p;\theta,\kappa)=H(p;1,\kappa/\theta),\qquad a(p;\theta,\kappa)=\theta\,a(p;1,\kappa/\theta).(75)

So the removal ratio rescales the pool in the symmetric-state analysis. The link gain at the symmetric state, and every instability threshold derived from it, are those of uniform removal with qP/Kq_P/K replaced by θqP/K\theta q_P/K and a by a/θa/\theta (exact, Figure 13). The substitution concerns the symmetric state only. It does not make whole trajectories or cycles identical, and eq. (74) is not the uniform ring with new constants.

The rescaling gives the two thresholds at once. The ring's symmetric state can lose stability exactly when θqP/K>7+43\theta q_P/K>7+4\sqrt3, by eq. (69). The symmetric state of the toggle of §16 is a saddle exactly when θqP/K>1\theta q_P/K>1 and

a>θ(θ+κθ−κ)2,a>\theta\Big(\frac{\theta+\kappa}{\theta-\kappa}\Big)^{2},(76)

which is eq. (43) rescaled. With bound repressor protected, θ=0\theta=0, eq. (75) gives

H=1−p∗<1H=1-p^*<1(77)

for every pool and production. Titration then lowers the production slope and the removal slope in the same proportion, and the two cancel. That is a local statement about the symmetric state. A global one also holds, because free-only removal turns each node into a Hill-1 filter of free repressor. Write node i in its free repressor yi=ϱ(ri)y_i=\varrho(r_i). Binding gives p=κ/(κ+y)p=\kappa/(\kappa+y), so the input of node i is a(κ/(κ+yi−1)+ε)a\big(\kappa/(\kappa+y_{i-1})+\varepsilon\big), a decreasing Möbius map of the upstream free repressor, and its removal ϱ(ri)\varrho(r_i) rises with rir_i. The limsup and liminf argument of the optional box in §24 then applies to the free repressors, around a ring of any length, odd or even. Every trajectory of the ring and of the toggle converges to the unique steady state, for every pool, production and leak (exact). A check from four starts at each of 24 parameter sets for the ring and the toggle found the same (numerical).

The numbers show how much protection the ring tolerates. At qP/K=200q_P/K=200 the largest leak-free gain is 7.11, 5.05, 3.24 and 1.74 for θ=1\theta=1, 0.5, 0.2 and 0.05 (exact). With a leak of 10−310^{-3} the values for 1, 0.5 and 0.05 are 6.99, 4.99 and 1.73 (numerical). The ring's steady state can lose stability only for θ>13.93/200=0.070\theta>13.93/200=0.070. At qP/K=50q_P/K=50 the bound repressor must leave at more than 0.279 times the rate of free repressor.

The published analyses sit at particular removal ratios. In Loinger and Biham's rate equations, bound repressor degrades at drd_r and free repressor at d, so θ=dr/d\theta=d_r/d. Without bound-repressor degradation their single steady state "is stable for any choice of the parameters" (p. 6), the case θ=0\theta=0. With it their Eq. 5 oscillates, and the oscillatory range "shrinks to zero when dr→0d_r\to0" (p. 7), consistent with the rescaled threshold.20 Müller and colleagues degrade free proteins only (preprint, p. 3), which is θ=0\theta=0, and find the central equilibrium of their ring stable for Hill coefficients below 4/3 (p. 29).21 Potvin-Trottier and colleagues note that equal dilution of repressor and binding sites is key to effective titration (Supplementary Information 4.3, p. 17).18

Name the bound-to-free removal ratio before deciding what monomeric repressors can do: replace qP/Kq_P/K by θqP/K\theta q_P/K in every symmetric-state threshold, so a toggle's symmetric state is a saddle only if θqP>K\theta q_P>K, a ring's rest state can lose stability only if θqP/K>7+43\theta q_P/K>7+4\sqrt3, and protected bound repressor allows neither a toggle nor a cycle.

28Hopf points, a subcritical edge and a relaxation cycle

Inside the window the ring settles onto a relaxation cycle. Its upper edge is subcritical, so a stable cycle outlives the unstable steady state, and rest and oscillation coexist.

5 · Close the loop. Take qP/K=200q_P/K=200 and a leak ε=10−3\varepsilon=10^{-3}. The steady state loses stability between two Hopf points, at a=2.094a=2.094 and a=226.2a=226.2, where the gain passes 2. The lower crossing is supercritical: the cycle grows from zero amplitude, with a peak-to-peak of 0.25 at a=2.105a=2.105. The upper crossing is subcritical. The large cycle outlives the steady state's instability up to a fold of cycles near a=408.7a=408.7, so a stable steady state and a stable cycle coexist for 226<a<409226<a<409, separated by an unstable cycle (all numerical). A gain above 2 is therefore sufficient for the steady state to lose stability, but not necessary for oscillation.

At the reference production the steady state spirals outward fast. At a=33.3a=33.3 the symmetric state has r∗=1.116r^*=1.116, p∗=0.0325p^*=0.0325 and H=5.81H=5.81. Eq. (62) then gives the eigenvalues −1−H=−6.81-1-H=-6.81 and −1+H/2±iH3/2=1.907±5.035i-1+H/2\pm iH\sqrt3/2=1.907\pm5.035i, which a finite-difference Jacobian reproduces (numerical).

The cycle is a relaxation oscillation through three titration switches. At a=33.3a=33.3 the period is 9.91/λ9.91/\lambda. Each total swings from 0.169 qP0.169\,q_P to 24.35 qP24.35\,q_P, while the free fraction of its target sites runs from 2×10−42\times10^{-4} to 0.83 (numerical, Figure 14). One repressor pulse holds the next promoter pool occupied while dilution clears it. When its total falls through the pool, the pool is released abruptly, the next gene fires, and its pulse represses the gene after. On the map of Figure 1, each pool sweeps its cut from far below the ray to far above it once per cycle. The same cycle is reached from a distant start.

Estimate: is the window within reach of a cell?

Take about 20 promoter copies per E. coli cell, which is about 20 nM by Lecture 2's rule that one molecule per cell is about one nanomolar. Take a tight repressor with K=0.1 nMK=0.1\ \mathrm{nM}. Then qP/K≈200q_P/K\approx200, far above 13.9. A free site that makes one repressor per minute, diluted at λ=0.03\lambda=0.03 per minute (a 23-minute doubling), gives a≈33a\approx33, inside the window 2<a<3862<a<386. The period is then 9.91/λ≈3309.91/\lambda\approx330 minutes, about 14 doublings. All of these are illustrative values and a model prediction.

For comparison, reported values. The Lac repressor binds its operator in vitro with a dissociation constant close to 10−13 M10^{-13}\ \mathrm M in standard buffer (p. 402).22 The chromosomal DnaA boxes of E. coli form a natural titration pool of about 300 high-affinity sites with dissociation constants near 1 nM (pp. 013011-2 to 013011-3).23 A three-node CRISPRi ring in E. coli oscillated with a period of 10 to 12 hours (p. 6).24 Clamons and Murray's full model predicts about seven hours (p. 12).

Loinger and Biham's oscillator sits inside the window. Their Fig. 2 uses one promoter site per gene, protein synthesis g=0.05g=0.05, degradation d=dr=0.003d=d_r=0.003, binding α0=0.5\alpha_0=0.5 per molecule and unbinding α1=0.01\alpha_1=0.01, all per second, and reports a period of about 2260 s (p. 19).20 In this page's units that is θ=1\theta=1, a=g/d=16.7a=g/d=16.7 and K=α1/α0=0.02K=\alpha_1/\alpha_0=0.02 molecules, so qP/K=50q_P/K=50. There the leak-free window is 2.43<a<85.62.43<a<85.6, the gain is 3.38, and eq. (67) cycles with period 7.02/λ=23397.02/\lambda=2339 s. Their binding is only a few times faster than degradation, so the occupancy constant (α1+dr)/α0=0.026(\alpha_1+d_r)/\alpha_0=0.026 is the better equilibrium proxy. With it qP/K=38.5q_P/K=38.5, the window is 2.60<a<62.42.60<a<62.4, the gain 2.95 and the period 2210 s (all numerical). The two equilibrium estimates bracket their reported period.

Read a ring's behavior from its closed dynamics, not from the gain alone: locate the two Hopf points and their criticality, expect a relaxation cycle with a period of about ten lifetimes inside the window, and check for a coexistence band beyond a subcritical edge.

29The cycle as a tour through repression patterns

The same cycle can be read without a Jacobian, as a sequence of repression patterns. The reading uses three kinds of statement, kept apart below: exact winner boundaries, asymptotic formulas on their own domains, and a high/low cartoon checked against the exact allocation.

A predicted rest point must pass two separate tests. It must be a fixed point of the coupled equations of its pattern and lie inside the inequalities that define that pattern, which is consistency. And it must be stable under the dynamics. Consistency alone proves nothing about memory or rest: a consistent point can be a saddle. The two tests are checked separately below.

Each link has two conservation rows, and each row has its own exact winner boundary. Take the pair formed by repressor Ri−1R_{i-1} and the sites of gene i, and write r=ri−1r=r_{i-1}. In units of qPq_P, the promoter row is 1=p+(1−p)1=p+(1-p), free sites plus bound sites, and the repressor row is r=ϱ+(1−p)r=\varrho+(1-p), free repressor plus bound copies. Free sites win the promoter row while p>1/2p>1/2, and putting p=1/2p=1/2 into p(r−1+p)=κ(1−p)p(r-1+p)=\kappa(1-p) gives r=1/2+κr=1/2+\kappa. Free repressor wins its row while ϱ>1−p\varrho>1-p, and with pϱ=κ(1−p)p\varrho=\kappa(1-p) the tie forces p=κp=\kappa, at r=2(1−κ)r=2(1-\kappa). At κ=0.005\kappa=0.005 the two boundaries are 0.505 and 1.99 (exact winner boundaries). Named by the winner of the promoter row and then of the repressor row, they split each link into (P,CPR)(P,C_{PR}) below 0.505, the singular (CPR,CPR)(C_{PR},C_{PR}) between, and (CPR,R)(C_{PR},R) above 1.99.

Each asymptotic formula holds on its own side of equivalence, not on its side of a winner boundary. Below equivalence, for 1−r≫κ1-r\gg\sqrt\kappa, the sites fill one for one and p≈1−rp\approx1-r. Above it, for r−1≫κr-1\gg\sqrt\kappa, the sites are full and p≈κ/(r−1)p\approx\kappa/(r-1). The exact quadratic (39) bridges the corner ∣r−1∣≲κ|r-1|\lesssim\sqrt\kappa, where neither piece holds. The excess formula has no meaning below equivalence, even inside the bound-sites regime: at r=0.75r=0.75 it gives p=−0.02p=-0.02, against the exact 0.26394345. Inserted into eq. (67), the two pieces give the reduced dynamics

1−ri−1≫κ:r˙i≈a(1−ri−1+ε)−ri,ri−1−1≫κ:r˙i≈a(κri−1−1+ε)−ri.\begin{aligned}&1-r_{i-1}\gg\sqrt\kappa:\qquad \dot r_i\approx a\big(1-r_{i-1}+\varepsilon\big)-r_i,\\ &r_{i-1}-1\gg\sqrt\kappa:\qquad \dot r_i\approx a\Big(\frac{\kappa}{r_{i-1}-1}+\varepsilon\Big)-r_i .\end{aligned}(78)

The first is affine in the totals. The second is nonlinear in the upstream total. Both relax rir_i at rate 1 toward a target set by the upstream total. At the two winner boundaries each piece is within 1.1% of the exact free fraction on its own side, and deeper inside it is closer (asymptotic formulas, on these domains).

The cartoon calls a repressor low below the promoter boundary and high above the repressor boundary. Low means r<0.505r<0.505, so its target sites are mostly free. High means r>1.99r>1.99, so it is mostly free itself and its target sites are nearly all bound. A repressor between the two boundaries is in the intermediate band, which the cartoon leaves unresolved. The band is much wider than the rounding layer ∣r−1∣≲κ≈0.07|r-1|\lesssim\sqrt\kappa\approx0.07, and away from that layer an asymptotic piece still works inside it: at r=0.7r=0.7, p≈1−r=0.3p\approx1-r=0.3 against the exact 0.311. This section simply uses the exact root throughout the band. The exact boundary values fix each node's target. A low upstream leaves p>1/2p>1/2, so the target a(p+ε)a(p+\varepsilon) lies between 16.68 and 33.33. A high upstream leaves p<κp<\kappa, so the target lies between 0.033 and 0.200 (exact, at a=33.3a=33.3, κ=0.005\kappa=0.005, ε=10−3\varepsilon=10^{-3}). For every production with 3.97<a<84.23.97<a<84.2, a low upstream sends its node's target into the high class, and a high upstream sends it into the low class.

No pattern of low and high repressors is consistent, so the ring cannot rest in one. In such a pattern each node heads for the class opposite to its upstream neighbour's, and around a ring of three no assignment of two classes alternates at every link. The two uniform patterns show the same through their coupled fixed points. In the all-low pattern every link follows the affine equation, and the coupled symmetric fixed point is r∗=a(1+ε)/(1+a)=0.97181633r^*=a(1+\varepsilon)/(1+a)=0.97181633, far above 0.505 and outside the affine piece's own domain (exact for eq. 78). The value a(1+ε)=33.3a(1+\varepsilon)=33.3 is only the target of a node whose upstream repressor is clamped at zero, and not a fixed point. In the all-high pattern the coupled symmetric fixed point solves r2−(1+aε)r+a(ε−κ)=0r^2-(1+a\varepsilon)r+a(\varepsilon-\kappa)=0, which gives r∗=1.149r^*=1.149, below 1.99 (exact for eq. 78). Neither reduced system has another fixed point, because each link is a decreasing affine or Möbius map of its upstream total.

The only steady state sits in the intermediate band, and the stability test rejects it. Each link of the full ring is a decreasing function of its upstream total, so the full ring has exactly one steady state, the symmetric one. At a=33.3a=33.3 it is r∗=1.116r^*=1.116, with p∗=0.0325p^*=0.0325. Bound sites hold 0.967 of the pool and bound copies 0.867 of the repressor, so every link is in the singular regime (CPR,CPR)(C_{PR},C_{PR}), inside the intermediate band and close to the rounding layer, at r∗−1≈1.6κr^*-1\approx1.6\sqrt\kappa. Neither asymptotic piece describes it: the excess piece gives a free fraction of 0.0430, against the exact 0.0325. The state is consistent and real, and its gain is H=5.81H=5.81, above the threshold of 2 from §24, so it is unstable (numerical). Consistency decides whether a predicted rest point is real. Stability decides whether the ring can stay there.

Between rest points the state is handed on, one release at a time. One repressor pulse holds the next promoter pool occupied while dilution clears it. When the pulse falls through the intermediate band, the pool is released, the next gene fires, and its pulse represses the gene after. Six phases of one period at a=33.3a=33.3, measured from a peak of r2r_2, give each repressor's class and the exact allocation of one promoter row and one repressor row:

The table checks the cartoon against the exact allocation. At every phase each low or high repressor is matched by its asymptotic piece to within 0.3% of the exact free fraction, and at three phases one repressor is crossing the intermediate band, where this section uses the exact root. Gene 1's promoter row changes winner twice per period, between free and bound sites. Repressor 1's row changes winner twice as well, between free repressor and the copies on gene 2's sites (numerical, in units of qPq_P). The cycle spans r from 0.169 to 24.35, so it crosses both exact boundaries, and the targets at its extremes, 27.7 from the trough and 0.040 from the peak, lie in the classes the cartoon predicts.

The pattern argument explains the order, and the full model supplies the rest. The reduced equations (78) hold on their domains and fail in the rounding layer around equivalence, which each repressor crosses twice per period, and the cartoon leaves the wider intermediate band unresolved. So the pattern argument explains the sequence of repression patterns, not the period, the amplitude or the basin. Those come from integrating the full ring, as §28 does, and the parameters used here are verified there to oscillate.

This is Marken, Xiao and Murray's structural reading, applied here to titration. They simplify a circuit inside each saturation regime, compute that regime's fixed point, and ask whether it is consistent, meaning that it lies inside the regime it came from (p. 8). For a Hill repressilator they find the all-low fixed point (α,α,α)(\alpha,\alpha,\alpha) inconsistent once α≫1\alpha\gg1, the all-high fixed point consistent but failing its own stability test once n≥2n\ge2, and the six mixed regimes pointing around the ring to carry the cycle (§4, pp. 12 to 14 and Fig. 4).26 Their all-low point does not transfer to this ring. It comes from production that is constant while the upstream repressor is low, whereas here production in the low class falls linearly with the upstream total, and the coupled all-low fixed point is a(1+ε)/(1+a)a(1+\varepsilon)/(1+a). What transfers is the pointing, here with no cooperativity at all. The bound a>3.97a>3.97, which sends a low upstream's target into the high class, plays the role of their α≫1\alpha\gg1, and the bound a<84.2a<84.2 keeps the target of a high upstream low against the leak and the residual free sites. The role of their consistent but unstable all-high point is taken by the steady state in the intermediate band, which lies near the rounding layer and needs the exact quadratic.

Their n≥2n\ge2 is a threshold of the limiting cartoon, not a finite-parameter condition. In the smooth Hill model at finite production the gain is H=np∗n/(1+p∗n)H=np^{*n}/(1+p^{*n}), below n by eq. (65), so at n=2n=2 the symmetric state's leading real part −1+H/2-1+H/2 is still negative. The cartoon is marginal exactly at that endpoint. The monomer ring has its own gain, eq. (42), and its own verified conditions, eq. (69) and the window (70). They are not the cartoon's condition transferred. They also state their own limits: the regime description is good far from a boundary and breaks down near one, smooth transitions between regimes are assumed rather than proved, and the connection between their structural matrix and the Jacobian is still under development (p. 15). Lecture 11 develops the systematic version of this method.

Read an oscillation as a tour through repression patterns: draw each pattern with exact winner boundaries, reduce its dynamics only where an asymptotic formula holds, compute the coupled fixed point before calling it a rest point, test consistency and stability separately, and keep the full model as the check on the period and the attractor.

Part 7

Every result holds in its regime

The five comparisons gave three kinds of contrast. Each sits at a regime boundary derived above. Collected, they place every example and every published result at its parameter conditions, invert into a list of requirements, and come with a precise guarantee and a precise limit.

30Three contrasts mark where an effective law leaves its regime

An effective law can hide a difference between mechanisms, forbid a behavior the mechanism produces, or misjudge how a capacity scales. In every case the law holds inside its regime, exactly in its limit and to leading order near it, and the contrast appears across a boundary with a formula.

The three kinds of contrast are the evidence, and each one has an address. The table lists, for each comparison, where the effective law holds and the boundary beyond which the binding-catalysis model parts from it.

The last row compares two architectures within one framework, not a mechanism with its own limit. The same-mechanism comparison for multistability is the monomeric toggle, in the fifth row.

The table mixes three kinds of boundary, and the difference matters. The validity boundary of an approximation, such as X∗≈qX∗X^*\approx q_X^* for the Michaelis-Menten law, ends a formula, not necessarily a behavior: a law can agree by accident outside its regime. A performance criterion, such as a tenfold-step error below 10%, is a threshold chosen by the test. A bifurcation boundary, such as the symmetric toggle's pitchfork, where its symmetric state becomes a saddle, or the ring's loss of stability, is a property of the closed dynamics. Rows 1 to 4 and 7 of the table are validity boundaries and performance criteria. Rows 5 and 6 are bifurcation boundaries.

Each boundary is a ratio of totals to an affinity, a removal ratio or a production window. None is a property of the effective law alone. Each names a parameter a cell or an experiment can move. That is why the contrasts can be turned into a placement: a published result is neither right nor wrong in general, it holds in the regime its conditions select.

Before calling an effective law wrong, find its regime and the boundary that ends it: a ratio of a total to a dissociation constant, a removal ratio, or a production window.
