The removal rule belongs on the map. Removal of free species alone protects bound molecules. That protection fixes the free-inducer steady state in §9, separates MultiFate's steady-state equations in §19, and forbids the monomeric toggle and ring in §27. Three of the table's rows change when θ\theta changes, so a placement that omits the removal rule is incomplete.

Some boundaries on the table come from the regimes and some from the closed dynamics. Where a half rise sits, where a window of adaptation ends, and where a switch occurs are read from the regimes of a binding pair. Where a steady state loses stability, eq. (69) and the window (70), is a condition on the Jacobian of the closed loop. It uses the exact titration slope across the singular ray, not a single regime's monomial law. §33 makes the distinction precise.

Place a new result by writing its mechanism as binding and catalysis, naming its removal ratio, and finding the row whose inequalities its parameters satisfy. If no row fits, run the five steps and add one.

32The same table, read as a set of requirements

Read from the behavior backwards, each row becomes a list of requirements on totals, affinities, production and removal, and an experiment that would show the boundary.

Inverting a row is a mechanical step, because every condition is an inequality in measurable quantities. Start from the behavior, find the rows that produce it, and read their inequalities as a specification. Each inequality names one of four things: which total is the controlled input, how large a total must be against a dissociation constant, how strong production must be against removal, and what the bound-to-free removal ratio must be. The last column then points at the derivation, so the requirement can be rechecked when a parameter is revised.

The requirements for the five behaviors of this chapter, stated as inequalities. A threshold in an induction input asks for the repressor architecture, an inducer whose total the system sets, and inducer binding tight enough for the sharpness wanted, which eq. (23) specifies. At the illustrated total qR=100KDRq_R=100K_{DR}, a ratio KRI/KDR=0.1K_{RI}/K_{DR}=0.1 gives nH≈6n_H\approx6, and the threshold sits at qRq_R (§7). A steep response from one binding layer asks for a titrant whose total sets the threshold and whose ratio to its KdK_d sets the sharpness, with c≪1c\ll1 and K2≪qRK_2\ll q_R for a two-site receptor (§13). Memory from monomeric parts asks, at the symmetric state, for θqP>K\theta q_P>K and production above eq. (76) (§16, §27). Adaptation of a total output is specified here by the test chosen in §21, a tenfold step held to 10%. For the degradation route it asks that the controller before the step stay below 0.0118Kd0.0118K_d in total, η≤0.0112\eta\le0.0112, and that catalysis be about 3500 times faster than any other removal of the output. For the repression route it asks that the controller exceed both KdK_d and the promoter total at the lowest input (§21, §22). A different step or tolerance moves these numbers. A cycle that grows from an unstable rest state asks for θqP/K>7+43\theta q_P/K>7+4\sqrt3, a production inside the window (70), and a small leak. A cycle can also coexist with a stable rest state beyond a subcritical edge, which none of these inequalities captures (§26 to §28).

Each requirement also names the sweep that would expose its boundary. The threshold row predicts that a sweep of the inducer total at several repressor totals moves the half rise with slope 1 in qRq_R. The receptor row predicts a peak at qR=qL/2q_R=q_L/2 when the receptor total is swept at fixed ligand. The adaptation rows predict opposite failures at the two ends of the input range, and different verdicts for the free and the total output. The ring rows predict a window in production with two edges, and a loss of the window as θ\theta falls. A measurement that follows a predicted boundary supports the placement. One that does not locates a missing state or a wrong removal rule, which is more useful than a better fit.

Two of these questions are handed forward. Lecture 10 takes the adaptation rows, with their scope: each design adapts over a feasible operating range of inputs, never over every input. Lecture 11 takes the regime maps themselves and develops the general geometry, for networks with many pairs, that this chapter uses one pair at a time.

Turn any row of the table into a specification by reading its inequalities as requirements on the controlled total, the ratios of totals to dissociation constants, the production window and the removal ratio, and then name the sweep that would show the boundary.

33What the regime enumeration guarantees, and what it leaves to the dynamics

For a written binding-catalysis mechanism, the regimes of its conservation sums can be enumerated completely. That covers the parameter space. It does not count attractors, locate Hopf points or decide whether a cycle coexists with a steady state.

The enumeration is complete because each conservation equation is a finite sum of positive terms. A mechanism fixes a finite list of species and a finite list of complexes, so each total is qi=∑jLijxjq_i=\sum_jL_{ij}x_j with LijL_{ij} the number of copies of constituent i in species j. At every positive parameter choice each such sum has a largest term, its winner. A choice of one winner per total is a regime, and there are finitely many choices. Enumerating them therefore exhausts the possibilities. Two kinds of inequality describe a regime, and only one is linear in the totals. The exact winner inequalities, such as CES>EC_{ES}>E, are linear in the logarithms of the species. Rewritten in the totals they generally are not: the exact tie of §2 lies on qS=Kd+qE/2q_S=K_d+q_E/2, which is not a line in log coordinates. The leading-order consistency conditions, written with each regime's own monomial laws, are linear inequalities in the logarithms of the totals and the binding constants, and they define the polyhedral map. Lecture 8 gives the procedure, and Lecture 11 develops its geometry.

The guarantee is conditional on the written mechanism being the intended one. The mechanism includes its binding states, its activities, its removal rules and the fast-equilibrium assumption. A missing complex, a missing conformation or a removal rule written as uniform when it is not changes the lists, and therefore the enumeration. Nothing in the procedure can detect such an omission. This chapter supplies three reminders: §19, where the removal rule changes the count from binomial sums to 1 or 2N2^N; §27, where the removal ratio rescales every symmetric-state threshold; and §22, where the promoter total, absent from the effective law, moves an adaptive window by a decade.

Three cases need the full equations rather than one regime's monomial law. The first is a tie, where two terms of one total contribute comparably. It marks a boundary between two regimes, and there either regime's law is off by a bounded factor, at most 2 for one pair (§2). The second is a singular regime, which is a different thing: its winners are dependent, as on §2's ray, where the complex wins both totals, the free pool is KdqE\sqrt{K_dq_E}, and the winner equations leave the free species undetermined until one more balance is added. The third is any question about the closed dynamics, which needs the Jacobian, built from exact slopes. The steep behavior lives near the first two: eq. (40)'s log-slope peaks at rpeakr_\mathrm{peak} of eq. (40a), just above equivalence.

The guarantee covers regimes, and the dynamics still decide the behavior. Four results of this chapter make the limit concrete. The number of stable states of MultiFate comes from enumerating fixed points of the closed loop and computing eigenvalues, not from the binding regimes (§19). The threshold qP/K>7+43q_P/K>7+4\sqrt3 comes from the Jacobian of the ring at its steady state, and it uses the exact titration slope (§26). The criticality of the two Hopf points, and the band from a=226a=226 to a=409a=409 where a stable cycle coexists with a stable steady state, come from integrating the closed dynamics (§28). And because of that subcritical edge, a gain above 2 is sufficient for the symmetric steady state to lose stability but not necessary for a cycle to exist. A complete regime analysis of a mechanism does not list its attractors.

So the chapter ends with one claim and one boundary on it. The claim: for a written binding-catalysis mechanism, the regimes of its conservation sums can be listed in full, every published result about its behaviors can be placed at the conditions where it holds, and the list inverts into requirements. The boundary: regimes are not attractors. Which attractor a closed loop reaches, whether a cycle exists, and whether rest and oscillation coexist are questions for the dynamics, answered example by example in Parts 4 to 6.

Claim completeness for the regimes of a written mechanism, under its stated binding states, activities, removal rules and equilibrium assumption, and claim nothing about attractors without the closed dynamics: stability, cycles and coexistence are separate calculations.

Part 8

Thresholds, gates and feedback

Four derivations that the core uses intuitively, each prompted by what the one before leaves open. Cooperative binding has an equilibrium ceiling on steepness, so §34 looks for a threshold in one binding pair read against a total. A threshold reads one input, so §35 asks what a promoter reading two inputs can compute. A steep law can be closed on its own output, so §36 asks what feedback buys from steepness, and finds a residual of about 1/(1+h)1/(1+h). That residual never vanishes, so §37 asks what removes it, and finds a stored difference of two sequestering species. Lecture 10 develops the adaptation story systematically.

34One binding pair computes a rectifier and a minimum

Why look for steepness in a single binding pair? Because occupancy at equilibrium, read against a free ligand, has a ceiling: its Hill slope cannot exceed the number of sites. One pair read against a total escapes that ceiling. With tight binding it leaves a free pool that is the positive part of a difference and a complex that is the smaller of two totals. Weak binding gives a product instead, and one bound covers the whole plane.

Cooperative occupancy has a ceiling on steepness, set by the number of sites. Take a molecule with n sites at equilibrium with a free ligand L, and let m be the number of ligands bound, distributed over the states with weights proportional to LmL^m. Then d⟨m⟩/dln⁡L=Var(m)d\langle m\rangle/d\ln L=\mathrm{Var}(m), and the Hill slope of the occupancy odds is

nH(L)=ddln⁡Lln⁡⟨m⟩n−⟨m⟩=n Var(m)⟨m⟩ (n−⟨m⟩)≤n.n_H(L)=\frac{d}{d\ln L}\ln\frac{\langle m\rangle}{n-\langle m\rangle}=\frac{n\,\mathrm{Var}(m)}{\langle m\rangle\,(n-\langle m\rangle)}\le n .(78a)

The bound holds because m lies between 0 and n, so ⟨m(n−m)⟩≥0\langle m(n-m)\rangle\ge0, which is Var(m)≤⟨m⟩(n−⟨m⟩)\mathrm{Var}(m)\le\langle m\rangle(n-\langle m\rangle). Equality needs all-or-none binding, every molecule empty or full. So a Hill slope of 8 by this route needs at least 8 sites on one molecule acting together, and reaching the bound needs all-or-none binding (exact, for direct occupancy at equilibrium). Sites are not subunits: one molecule can carry several sites, so the count says nothing about how many proteins assemble. This is an equilibrium limit of the kind Lecture 7 contrasted with driven mechanisms.

The ceiling binds one kind of mechanism, and a fitted coefficient does not reveal the mechanism. Eq. (78a) concerns direct occupancy at equilibrium, read against the free ligand. A large fitted Hill coefficient therefore does not by itself imply that many sites. This chapter has already passed the ceiling twice: §11 with saturated enzymes, which are driven, and §13 with two sites read against a ligand total. Titration passes it the second way, by changing the input from a free ligand to a total, and one binding pair shows how.

The exact pair is one root, and every limit below is a limit of it. Take A+B⇌k−k+CABA+B\xrightleftharpoons[k_-]{k_+}C_{AB} with Kd=k−/k+K_d=k_-/k_+, totals qA=A+CABq_A=A+C_{AB} and qB=B+CABq_B=B+C_{AB}, and equilibrium KdCAB=ABK_dC_{AB}=AB. As in eq. (4),

CAB=2qAqBT+T2−4qAqB,T=qA+qB+Kd.C_{AB}=\frac{2q_Aq_B}{T+\sqrt{T^2-4q_Aq_B}},\qquad T=q_A+q_B+K_d .(79)

Tight binding gives a rectifier and a minimum. Let Kd→0K_d\to0 at fixed totals. Then AB=KdCAB→0AB=K_dC_{AB}\to0, so at least one free pool vanishes, while the exact difference qA−qB=A−Bq_A-q_B=A-B is preserved. If qA>qBq_A>q_B then B vanishes and A→qA−qBA\to q_A-q_B, and otherwise A vanishes. So

A→max⁡(0, qA−qB),B→max⁡(0, qB−qA),CAB→min⁡(qA,qB).A\to\max(0,\,q_A-q_B),\qquad B\to\max(0,\,q_B-q_A),\qquad C_{AB}\to\min(q_A,q_B).(80)

The free pool is a rectifier in the partner total: zero up to a threshold at qBq_B, then linear with slope 1. The complex is the smaller of the two totals, the limiting-pool response. These are the two readouts of §2's tight cut, written as functions.

At the corner the rectifier is rounded, and the rounding has a size. Set qA=qB=qq_A=q_B=q in eq. (79). Then A=BA=B and A2=KdCAB=Kd(q−A)A^2=K_dC_{AB}=K_d(q-A), so A=(Kd2+4Kdq−Kd)/2≈KdqA=\big(\sqrt{K_d^2+4K_dq}-K_d\big)/2\approx\sqrt{K_dq} when Kd≪qK_d\ll q (exact root, leading-order value). At qB=1q_B=1 and Kd=10−4K_d=10^{-4} the exact free pool is 0.00995 against KdqB=0.01\sqrt{K_dq_B}=0.01 (numerical). The rectifier's corner is therefore not sharp: it is rounded over a width of order KdqB\sqrt{K_dq_B} in the totals.

The log gain at the corner is the same 12qB/Kd\tfrac12\sqrt{q_B/K_d} that Part 4 found, from one site. Differentiating the free pool with respect to qAq_A at qA=qBq_A=q_B gives a log gain of 50.50 at qB/Kd=104q_B/K_d=10^4, against 12qB/Kd=50\tfrac12\sqrt{q_B/K_d}=50 (numerical). One site per molecule, read against a total, so the ceiling of eq. (78a) does not apply, and the steepness grows without bound as binding tightens. The free fraction of a promoter pool in §16 is this same free pool with qBq_B the pool and qAq_A the repressor, which is why its peak slope has the same form.

Weak binding gives a product. If both totals are far below KdK_d, both free pools are nearly their totals and CAB≈qAqB/KdC_{AB}\approx q_Aq_B/K_d, a multiplier. So one pair computes a product, a minimum or a rectified difference, depending only on where the two totals sit against KdK_d.

One bound covers the whole plane. The three limits are the three candidates qAq_A, qBq_B and qAqB/Kdq_Aq_B/K_d, and for positive totals and KdK_d the complex is never far from the smallest of them:

3−52≤CABmin⁡(qA, qB, qAqB/Kd)≤1,3−52=0.38197.\frac{3-\sqrt5}{2}\le\frac{C_{AB}}{\min\big(q_A,\ q_B,\ q_Aq_B/K_d\big)}\le1 ,\qquad \frac{3-\sqrt5}{2}=0.38197 .(81)

The upper bound is immediate: CABC_{AB} cannot exceed either total, and KdCAB=AB≤qAqBK_dC_{AB}=AB\le q_Aq_B. The lower bound needs a short argument, in two steps: rescale by the minimum, then bound the binding quadratic at one point. Let m=min⁡(qA,qB,qAqB/Kd)m=\min(q_A,q_B,q_Aq_B/K_d), and write a=qA/ma=q_A/m, b=qB/mb=q_B/m, z=CAB/mz=C_{AB}/m and k=Kd/mk=K_d/m. Then a,b≥1a,b\ge1 and k≤abk\le ab, because m≤qAqB/Kdm\le q_Aq_B/K_d. Equilibrium becomes g(z)=(a−z)(b−z)−kz=0g(z)=(a-z)(b-z)-kz=0, and the physical root is the one below min⁡(a,b)\min(a,b), where g falls from g(0)=ab>0g(0)=ab>0. It suffices to show g(c)≥0g(c)\ge0 at c=(3−5)/2c=(3-\sqrt5)/2, for then the root lies at or above c. Using k≤abk\le ab,

g(c)≥(a−c)(b−c)−c ab=ab[1−c−ca−cb+c2ab].g(c)\ge(a-c)(b-c)-c\,ab=ab\Big[1-c-\frac ca-\frac cb+\frac{c^2}{ab}\Big].(81a)

The bracket is linear in each of 1/a1/a and 1/b1/b, which lie in (0,1](0,1], so its minimum sits at a corner. The corner (1,1)(1,1) gives 1−3c+c21-3c+c^2, which is zero because c is the smaller root of c2−3c+1=0c^2-3c+1=0, and the other corners give 1−2c1-2c and 1−c1-c, both positive. So z≥cz\ge c, with equality only at a=b=1a=b=1 and k=abk=ab, that is qA=qB=Kdq_A=q_B=K_d (exact). A scan of 61361^3 points over six decades in each of qAq_A, qBq_B and KdK_d agrees, with the ratio between 0.38197 and 1.0000 (numerical). So the three-way minimum is a leading-order law whose error is a factor of at most 2.62 anywhere, which is the bounded-factor accuracy of a dominance regime made concrete.

Read one binding pair as three computations selected by the totals: a product below KdK_d, a minimum above it, and a rectified difference in the free pool, with a corner rounded over KdqB\sqrt{K_dq_B}, a steepness that passes the equilibrium site ceiling because the input is a total, and a three-way minimum accurate within the factor 2.62 of eq. (81).

35A two-input promoter computes a gate set by its activities

A threshold reads one input. What can a promoter that reads two inputs compute? Its four binding states and their activities decide the gate. The truth table is a regime table of the promoter's conservation sum, and the gate has a fixed sign in each input exactly when its activities satisfy two inequalities per input.

The model is one conservation sum over four states. A promoter G binds regulator A at one site and regulator B at another, independently, with dissociation constants KAK_A and KBK_B. Independence means that each site binds with the same constants whether or not the other is occupied, so the four elementary steps close a square of states. Transcription from any state is composite:

G+A⇌k−Ak+ACGA,CGB+A⇌k−Ak+ACGAB,G+B⇌k−Bk+BCGB,CGA+B⇌k−Bk+BCGAB,qG=G+CGA+CGB+CGAB,v=a00G+a10CGA+a01CGB+a11CGAB.\begin{aligned}&G+A\xrightleftharpoons[k_{-A}]{k_{+A}}C_{GA},\qquad C_{GB}+A\xrightleftharpoons[k_{-A}]{k_{+A}}C_{GAB},\\ &G+B\xrightleftharpoons[k_{-B}]{k_{+B}}C_{GB},\qquad C_{GA}+B\xrightleftharpoons[k_{-B}]{k_{+B}}C_{GAB},\\ &q_G=G+C_{GA}+C_{GB}+C_{GAB},\qquad v=a_{00}G+a_{10}C_{GA}+a_{01}C_{GB}+a_{11}C_{GAB}.\end{aligned}(82)

Here a00a_{00}, a10a_{10}, a01a_{01} and a11a_{11} are the transcription activities of the empty, A-bound, B-bound and doubly bound states. Independent binding does not make the activities independent: any four values are allowed. At equilibrium the four states are in proportion 1:x:y:xy1:x:y:xy, with x=A/KAx=A/K_A and y=B/KBy=B/K_B, so

vqG=a00+a10x+a01y+a11xy(1+x)(1+y).\frac{v}{q_G}=\frac{a_{00}+a_{10}x+a_{01}y+a_{11}xy}{(1+x)(1+y)}.(83)

An on-off gate gives each activity the value a or 0, and the set A\mathcal A of expressing states names the gate.

The truth table is the regime table of the promoter total. Take each input either far below its dissociation constant, written 0, or far above it, written 1. At each corner one term of (1+x)(1+y)(1+x)(1+y) dominates, so one state wins the promoter total: the empty state at (0,0), the A-bound state at (1,0), the B-bound state at (0,1) and the doubly bound state at (1,1). The output is then the activity of that winner. Five gates follow at once:

Expressing states A\mathcal A(0,0)(1,0)(0,1)(1,1)Gate
{AB}\{AB\}0001AND
{A,B,AB}\{A,B,AB\}0111OR
{∅}\{\varnothing\}1000NOR
{∅,A,B}\{\varnothing,A,B\}1110NAND
{A}\{A\}0100A AND NOT B

Reading a gate off a promoter is therefore the same exercise as reading a regime off a conservation sum: name the winner at each corner, then look up its activity.

The corners are idealizations, and each transition has a width set by its dissociation constant. With free inputs each site's occupancy is x/(1+x)x/(1+x), which rises from 10% to 90% over a factor of 81 in its input, centred on its K. A corner is reached only when each input is far from its dissociation constant. If a regulator is depleted by the promoter, its input becomes a total, and the tight-titration rounding of §34, of order Kq\sqrt{Kq}, replaces that width. A gate drawn as a truth table is an assertion about the corners alone.

The sign of each input is fixed by two inequalities on the activities. Differentiating eq. (83) in x at fixed y,

∂∂x vqG=(a10−a00)+(a11−a01) y(1+x)2(1+y).\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\,\frac{v}{q_G}=\frac{(a_{10}-a_{00})+(a_{11}-a_{01})\,y}{(1+x)^2(1+y)}.(84)

The sign is that of a straight line in y. So A activates at every level of B exactly when a10≥a00a_{10}\ge a_{00} and a11≥a01a_{11}\ge a_{01}, and represses at every level exactly when both inequalities reverse. B has the two corresponding inequalities, a01≥a00a_{01}\ge a_{00} and a11≥a10a_{11}\ge a_{10} for activation. The five gates of the table satisfy them, each input with one sign. A fixed-sign gate is monotone in each input, and it is these activity inequalities, not the positivity of the activities, that make it so.

XOR breaks the inequalities, and one layer can still compute it. XOR expresses at (1,0) and (0,1) and not at (0,0) or (1,1). Take A={A,B}\mathcal A=\{A,B\}: a10=a01=aa_{10}=a_{01}=a and a00=a11=0a_{00}=a_{11}=0, a silent doubly bound state. Eq. (84) becomes a(1−y)/((1+x)2(1+y))a(1-y)/\big((1+x)^2(1+y)\big), which changes sign at y=1y=1, that is B=KBB=K_B, so B decides whether A activates or represses (exact). The four corners give 0, 1, 1 and 0. XOR therefore needs no new binding model, only this activity assignment, which violates a11≥a01a_{11}\ge a_{01}. Mutual exclusion alone does not give it: without the doubly bound state, the A-bound or B-bound state wins at (1,1), that corner expresses, and the gate becomes OR. Whether a real promoter silences its doubly bound state while expressing from each single state is a question about its activities. The alternative is a second layer, with one promoter computing OR, another NAND, and a third taking their outputs through an AND. Lecture 12 develops cellular computation.

Read a promoter gate from the winner of its conservation sum at each input corner, and read the sign of each input from the activity inequalities of eq. (84): XOR, which violates them, needs a silent doubly bound state or a second layer.

36Negative feedback divides small disturbances and small inputs by the same factor

§34 and §35 read their inputs without feedback. Closing a steep law on its own output asks a new question: how far does the steepness protect a steady state? Locally, one scalar identity divides a small change of removal and a small change of input by the same factor, 1+h1+h. A finite change needs that identity integrated, because h moves with the steady state.

The model is one species with a decreasing production law. Let an input u drive production through a decreasing function F, and let the species be removed at frequency δ\delta:

x˙=u F(x)−δx,F>0, F′<0.\dot x=u\,F(x)-\delta x,\qquad F>0,\ F'<0 .(85)

The production law F is the negative feedback: more x makes less x. At a positive steady state uF(x∗)=δx∗uF(x^*)=\delta x^*, define the static feedback steepness

h=−x∗F′(x∗)F(x∗) ≥0.h=-\frac{x^*F'(x^*)}{F(x^*)}\ \ge0 .(86)

For a Hill law F(x)=1/(1+(x/K)n)F(x)=1/(1+(x/K)^n), h is n(x∗/K)n/(1+(x∗/K)n)n(x^*/K)^n/(1+(x^*/K)^n), below n, as in eq. (65). It is the same kind of quantity as the link gain H of §24, a log-slope of production. In this one-species loop the link is the whole loop, so h is also its loop gain. The lower-case h keeps the one-species loop apart from the three-node ring.

Implicit differentiation gives both local sensitivities at once. Take the logarithm of the balance: ln⁡u+ln⁡F(x∗)=ln⁡δ+ln⁡x∗\ln u+\ln F(x^*)=\ln\delta+\ln x^*. Differentiating, and using dln⁡F=−h dln⁡x∗d\ln F=-h\,d\ln x^*,

dln⁡u−h dln⁡x∗=dln⁡δ+dln⁡x∗,sodln⁡x∗dln⁡δ=−11+h,dln⁡x∗dln⁡u=+11+h.d\ln u-h\,d\ln x^*=d\ln\delta+d\ln x^*,\qquad\text{so}\qquad \frac{d\ln x^*}{d\ln\delta}=-\frac{1}{1+h},\qquad \frac{d\ln x^*}{d\ln u}=+\frac{1}{1+h}.(87)

Without feedback, h=0h=0, the steady state is inversely proportional to the removal rate, for any change. With h=9h=9, a small relative change of the removal rate moves the steady state by a tenth as much. Checked against finite differences of exact steady states of eq. (85) for Hill laws with n=1n=1, 2 and 4, the identities agree to 10 significant figures (numerical).

A finite change needs the identity integrated, because h moves with the steady state. Integrating eq. (87) along the path from δ1\delta_1 to δ2\delta_2,

ln⁡x2∗x1∗=−∫δ1δ211+h(x∗(δ)) dln⁡δ.\ln\frac{x_2^*}{x_1^*}=-\int_{\delta_1}^{\delta_2}\frac{1}{1+h\big(x^*(\delta)\big)}\,d\ln\delta .(87a)

The power law (δ2/δ1)−1/(1+h)(\delta_2/\delta_1)^{-1/(1+h)} follows only if h is constant along the whole path, and a Hill law's h is not: it falls as the steady state falls. Take F=1/(1+x16)F=1/(1+x^{16}), δ1=1\delta_1=1 and the steady state with h=9h=9, which is x1∗=(9/7)1/16x_1^*=(9/7)^{1/16} with u=x1∗(1+x1∗16)u=x_1^*(1+x_1^{*16}). Doubling δ\delta gives x2∗/x1∗=0.905415x_2^*/x_1^*=0.905415, against 0.933033 from a frozen h. A tenfold increase gives 0.228571, against 0.794328 (exact steady states of eq. 85). Steepness protects a steady state only while the steady state stays on the steep part of its law.

The same steepness that rejects a disturbance also rejects the signal. Eqs. (87) are equal and opposite. Locally, a loop that suppresses a change in its removal rate by 1/(1+h)1/(1+h) suppresses a change in its input by exactly the same factor. Rejection and responsiveness are the same quantity here, which is why a circuit that must both hold a set point and follow a signal cannot do it with static steepness alone.

The steady state of this scalar model is always locally stable. Linearizing eq. (85) at x∗x^* gives the eigenvalue uF′(x∗)−δuF'(x^*)-\delta, which is negative because F′<0F'<0. So negative feedback in this one-species, instantaneous form cannot destabilize anything. That is a property of the scalar model, not of feedback in general: Part 6's ring is negative feedback with three stages, and it oscillates.

The electronic form of the statement carries two different gains, and they must not be confused. In Black's static amplifier an input u is amplified by A after a fraction β\beta of the output is subtracted. This β\beta is a feedback factor, not the Hill coefficient of §15 or the activated production of §18. The relation is y=A(u−βy)y=A(u-\beta y). Solving,

yu=A1+Aβ,dln⁡(y/u)dln⁡A=11+Aβ.\frac{y}{u}=\frac{A}{1+A\beta},\qquad \frac{d\ln(y/u)}{d\ln A}=\frac{1}{1+A\beta}.(88)

The first quantity is the closed-loop gain, which falls as feedback is added. The second is the relative sensitivity of that gain to the amplifier, which falls in the same proportion. At A=100A=100 and β=1\beta=1 the closed-loop gain is 0.990 and the sensitivity is 0.0099 (exact). Black wrote the same two relations as μ/(1−μβ)\mu/(1-\mu\beta) and (δμ/μ)/(1−μβ)(\delta\mu/\mu)/(1-\mu\beta), with his loop transmission μβ\mu\beta negative for negative feedback (pp. 5 to 6).27 Writing AβA\beta as the loop gain, eq. (88) has the form of eq. (87) with h=Aβh=A\beta: locally, a loop gain of h divides a change by 1+h1+h. Khammash draws the same comparison for a negatively autoregulated gene with Hill coefficient n, whose steady state has sensitivities of about ±1/(n+1)\pm1/(n+1) to its expression and degradation rates (Fig. 2 caption, p. 5).28 That is the limit h→nh\to n of eq. (87), reached at high expression.

Measure what negative feedback buys from the static steepness h=−x∗F′/Fh=-x^*F'/F: locally it divides both a disturbance and an input by 1+h1+h, a finite change needs the integral (87a) because h moves with the steady state, and in the scalar model feedback never costs stability.

37Rejection is not perfect adaptation

§36's loop shrinks an error but never removes it. What removes it? A stored quantity, not a steeper curve. Two sequestering species supply one: the rate of change of their difference is the error, so the difference stores the accumulated error, and at a steady state the error is zero.

A static law cannot reach zero error at finite steepness. By eq. (87a) a finite change of the removal rate leaves the steady state unchanged only if h is infinite along the whole path. Locally the residual is the fraction 1/(1+h)1/(1+h) of the change. For a large step it can be much worse, because h falls as the steady state falls: in §36's example a tenfold step from h=9h=9 leaves the output at 0.229 of its old level. The binding mechanisms of Parts 3 and 4 supply a finite h: eq. (40a) caps the titration steepness at (1+κ)/(2κ)(1+\kappa)/(2\sqrt\kappa), and eq. (65) caps a Hill law below its coefficient.

Integral action is a stored quantity, and that is a different thing from a steep curve. An integrator holds a running total of the error and keeps changing its output until that error is zero. The state that holds it is a memory, so the circuit needs an extra species, not a sharper function of x. Khammash describes the same action in the frequency domain, as infinite gain at zero frequency (p. 7).28 That description belongs to a dynamic integrator, and it is not a licence to treat an infinitely steep static law as one.

Sequestration supplies the memory, written here as a reversible pair whose complex is removed. A reference species Z1Z_1 is made at constant rate μ\mu and actuates the output. A sensor species Z2Z_2 is made in proportion to the output, at rate θX\theta X. The two bind into a complex, which is removed. This θ\theta is the controller's sensing rate, in the notation of Briat, Gupta and Khammash, and not the bound-to-free removal ratio of §27, which does not appear again in this section.29 The output X is made by free Z1Z_1 and removed at frequency γ\gamma, and the disturbance is a change of γ\gamma:

∅⇝Z1  (rate law μ),X⇝X+Z2  (rate law θX),Z1+Z2⇌k−k+CZ1Z2,CZ1Z2⇝∅  (rate law δCCZ1Z2),Z1⇝Z1+X  (rate law kZ1),X⇝∅  (rate law γX).\begin{aligned}&\varnothing\rightsquigarrow Z_1\ \ (\text{rate law }\mu),\qquad X\rightsquigarrow X+Z_2\ \ (\text{rate law }\theta X),\qquad Z_1+Z_2\xrightleftharpoons[k_-]{k_+}C_{Z_1Z_2},\\ &C_{Z_1Z_2}\rightsquigarrow\varnothing\ \ (\text{rate law }\delta_CC_{Z_1Z_2}),\qquad Z_1\rightsquigarrow Z_1+X\ \ (\text{rate law }kZ_1),\qquad X\rightsquigarrow\varnothing\ \ (\text{rate law }\gamma X).\end{aligned}(89)

Binding and unbinding cancel in the difference of the two free species. The net sequestration flux k+Z1Z2−k−CZ1Z2k_+Z_1Z_2-k_-C_{Z_1Z_2} takes one Z1Z_1 and one Z2Z_2 per binding event and returns one of each per unbinding, so it enters both free balances identically:

d(Z1−Z2)dt=μ−θX.\frac{d(Z_1-Z_2)}{dt}=\mu-\theta X .(90)

The rate of change of Z1−Z2Z_1-Z_2 is the error μ−θX\mu-\theta X, so Z1−Z2Z_1-Z_2 itself stores the accumulated error. With the totals qZ1=Z1+CZ1Z2q_{Z_1}=Z_1+C_{Z_1Z_2} and qZ2=Z2+CZ1Z2q_{Z_2}=Z_2+C_{Z_1Z_2}, the difference is also qZ1−qZ2q_{Z_1}-q_{Z_2}, and complex removal, which takes one of each, cancels there too. At any steady state the left side of eq. (90) is zero, so

X∗=μθ,X^*=\frac{\mu}{\theta},(91)

whatever γ\gamma and the plant's other constants are. This is robust perfect adaptation: the set point depends on two controller constants and on nothing in the controlled network. Simulating eq. (89) at μ=2\mu=2, θ=0.5\theta=0.5, k+=10k_+=10, k−=1k_-=1, δC=0.5\delta_C=0.5 and k=1k=1, from small positive starts, the steady state is 4.000000 at γ=0.5\gamma=0.5, 1, 2 and 3, and every species stays nonnegative (numerical). Briat and colleagues write the comparison as annihilation, Z1+Z2→∅Z_1+Z_2\to\varnothing, an event that lowers both counts by one and so preserves their difference (Equation 1, p. 19). Eq. (90) holds there too, but annihilation conserves no separate totals.

At steady state the free reference is §34's rectifier, with an effective constant that includes removal. The complex balance at a steady state of eq. (89) gives Z1Z2=KeffCZ1Z2Z_1Z_2=K_\mathrm{eff}C_{Z_1Z_2} with Keff=(k−+δC)/k+K_\mathrm{eff}=(k_-+\delta_C)/k_+, because removal empties the complex as unbinding does. When KeffK_\mathrm{eff} is small against the totals, eq. (80) applied with KeffK_\mathrm{eff} gives Z1≈max⁡(0,qZ1−qZ2)Z_1\approx\max(0,q_{Z_1}-q_{Z_2}): the actuator runs only while the reference total exceeds the sensor total. A small k−/k+k_-/k_+ alone is not enough. At μ=θ=k=γ=k+=1\mu=\theta=k=\gamma=k_+=1, k−=10−6k_-=10^{-6} and δC=100\delta_C=100, the steady state has Z1=1Z_1=1 while qZ1−qZ2=−10−8q_{Z_1}-q_{Z_2}=-10^{-8}, because Keff=100K_\mathrm{eff}=100 (exact). Using the equilibrium constant k−/k+k_-/k_+ along a transient also needs binding fast against complex removal. The memory identity (90) needs neither approximation, and the zero steady error comes from it, not from the sharpness of the corner.

Three conditions belong next to that claim: the loop must settle, a reversible complex must be removed, and the free controller species must not be. Take settling first. Eq. (91) holds at a steady state, and the difference balance says nothing about whether the loop reaches one. "If it settles" is a stability condition on the full closed loop, as everywhere in this chapter. Briat and colleagues prove settling, in the stochastic sense of ergodicity, for unimolecular networks whose open loop is stable and output controllable and whose set point is accessible (Theorem 2, p. 21). They also note that the deterministic counterpart can oscillate in an instability region (p. 24).

A reversible complex must be removed, or the loop has no steady state. Without complex removal nothing removes the reference, so qZ1q_{Z_1} grows as μt\mu t. The complex then grows as μt\mu t too, and the free sensor must grow with it to keep binding balanced against unbinding. With K=k−/k+K=k_-/k_+ its growth rate is Kμ/Zˉ1K\mu/\bar Z_1, which the sensor's production θXˉ\theta\bar X must supply on top of μ\mu. The output therefore settles at an offset instead of the set point,

Xˉ=μθ(1+KZˉ1),Zˉ1=γXˉk,\bar X=\frac{\mu}{\theta}\Big(1+\frac{K}{\bar Z_1}\Big),\qquad \bar Z_1=\frac{\gamma\bar X}{k},

which is 4.0976 at γ=1\gamma=1 and 4.0331 at γ=3\gamma=3 with δC=0\delta_C=0 and the other constants above (exact for this ramp, and numerical). The plant's removal rate now sets the output, so adaptation is lost. Irreversible binding into an inert complex, k−=0k_-=0, needs no removal, because the complex never returns its partners. Annihilation is that case.

Removing the complex does not leak the memory, but removing the free controller species does. The cancellation in eq. (90) is a cancellation of equal event fluxes: each binding, unbinding or complex-removal event changes the two free species, or the two totals, by the same amount. Equal first-order removal of the free species is not such a flux. Diluting free Z1Z_1 and Z2Z_2 at δZ\delta_Z gives d(Z1−Z2)/dt=μ−θX−δZ(Z1−Z2)d(Z_1-Z_2)/dt=\mu-\theta X-\delta_Z(Z_1-Z_2), a leaky integrator, and the set point acquires an offset: the output falls from 4.000 to 3.925 at δZ=0.01\delta_Z=0.01 and to 3.358 at 0.1 (numerical). As in §27, the removal rule is part of the model, and here equal dilution of the two free species is enough to make the memory leak.

A living cell dilutes its controller, so its adaptation is near-perfect rather than exact. Aoki and colleagues built the motif in E. coli from the σ factor SigW and its anti-σ factor RsiW. They note that the theory assumes unsaturated production and negligible degradation of the two controller proteins, that living cells satisfy neither, and that simulations with realistic parameters gave small errors (p. 535).30 In eq. (90) that is the leak term.

Lecture 10 takes this question up systematically. It develops the internal model principle, the conditions for robust perfect adaptation, chemotaxis and the comparison with the feedforward designs of Part 5. This section supplies only the two identities, eq. (87) for static rejection and eq. (90) for stored memory, and the distinction between them.

Separate three quantities: the static steepness h, which divides a small disturbance by 1+h1+h; a stored difference, whose rate of change is the error and which drives the error to zero through eq. (90); and the stability of the closed loop, which neither of them establishes. Keep a reversible complex removed and the free controller species unremoved, or the memory fails.
